Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES AUTHORITY FOR EXTENSION BEYOND THE CONFINES OF CANADA
speechtext: Will the minister explain the resolution, please?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES AUTHORITY FOR EXTENSION BEYOND THE CONFINES OF CANADA
speechtext:
The amendments are very simple. They are to correct two omissions in the original bill. By agreement made some two years ago with Great Britain, Ireland and Newfoundland, Canada is obligated to take a proportion of stock in the Transatlantic Air Service. The agreement provided that each government should nominate an aviation company which would assume the government obligation in that regard, and the amendment provides that authority shall be given to Trans-Canada Air Lines to purchase the government's share of stock in that company. When we were discussing the bill itself last year I mentioned that this would be the company entrusted with that service, and in setting up the capital of the company, funds were provided to carry out this obligation, but we omitted to provide in the bill that the company should have the right to purchase the government share of stock in the transatlantic company.
The second amendment is also to correct an omission. It will be recalled by hon. members that the route of Trans-Canada Air Lines was originally laid out across the state of Maine between Montreal and Moncton, New Brunswick. A strict reading of the act that was passed last year would prohibit Trans-Canada Air Lines from operating outside Canada, and the amendment makes a very minor alteration to permit the company to operate outside of Canada, either on the main transcontinental route or with such international connections as the government may designate in the operation of the service.

Hon. FERNAND RINFRET (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 22, respecting the registration of shop cards by labour unions.
He said: This is a bill to enable the registration of shop cards by labour unions with the Department of the Secretary of
Shop Cards Registration

State. This is not a new matter. As far back as the session of 1927, on March 25, the then minister of labour, Hon. Peter Heenan, introduced a bill to amend the Trade Mark and Design Act to permit the very same object [DOT]we have in view in the present bill. But in 1932 the former secretary of state had the house adopt, under the title of the Unfair Competition Act, an act defining the wares that may be registered by trade marks, and although that measure did not positively so state, it excluded by its very operation the registration of shop cards and union labels that were not actually attached to wares.
The bill introduced by the former secretary of state and passed was the sequel to an international conference which took place at the Hague in 1925, and the bill was passed pursuant to the conclusions arrived at at that conference, where it had been expressly desired that the trade mark should apply to goods and to wares and not to any quality of work irrespective of the object or ware. The definition given in the Unfair Competition Act, 1932, of a trade mark was as follows:
"Trade mark" means a symbol which has become adapted to distinguish particular wares falling within a general category from other wares falling within the same category, and is used by any person in association with wares entering into trade or commerce for the purpose of indicating to dealers in. and/or users [DOT]of such wares that they have been manufactured, sold, leased or hired by him, or that they are of a defined standard or have been produced under defined working conditions, by a defined class of persons, or in a defined territorial area, and includes any distinguishing . [DOT]guise capable of constituting a trade mark.
By the act of 1932, therefore, the registration of a trade mark was confined solely to wares or goods, and it made impossible any further registration of shop cards or union labels such as had been provided for by the [DOT]amending bill of 1927.

subsubtopic: CARDS OF LABOUR UNIONS AND PREVENTING UNAUTHORIZED USE
speechtext: Is not that the definition -given by the international conference?

subsubtopic: CARDS OF LABOUR UNIONS AND PREVENTING UNAUTHORIZED USE
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: CARDS OF LABOUR UNIONS AND PREVENTING UNAUTHORIZED USE
speechtext: Well, how can we depart from it?

subsubtopic: CARDS OF LABOUR UNIONS AND PREVENTING UNAUTHORIZED USE
speechtext:
That is the reason why
the bill as introduced now is a different bill .[DOT]altogether. It provides for similar procedure, but distinct, and has nothing to do with the Unfair Competition Act, which deals strictly with trade marks as provided for at the conference to which I have just alluded.
Between 1927 and 1932, when the new act was introduced and passed, a certain number of registrations of shop cards and union labels were made. There were not a great number

of them, but it may be of interest to the house to know that in 1928 eleven such registrations took place; in 1929, five more; two in 1930, and two in 1931, a total of twenty registrations of shop cards or labels made during that period. Inasmuch as the registration is made for fifteen years, those still exist with the department. It was provided in the act of 1932 that no further registration should take place except within the meaning of the act, but it maintained the registrations that had already been entered. Section 23, subsection 1 of that act is as follows:
The register now existing under the Trade Mark and Design Act shall form part of the register maintained pursuant to this act, and, subject as hereinafter provided, all entries therein shall hereafter be governed by the provisions of this act, but shall not, if properly made under the law in force at the time they were made, he subject to be expunged or amended only because they might not properly have been made hereunder.
It will therefore be seen that the registrations entered before 1932 are still in force.
The object of introducing this bill is to meet wishes repeatedly expressed by labour unions and labour associations when they have come before the government. I shall not quote them all, but I may perhaps allude to the memorandum of legislative program presented to the cabinet by the executive council of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada on Friday, December 18, 1936. The paragraph relating to this bill reads as follows:
Further Protection for Union Services:-At present the Unfair Competition Act protects the use of the union label, but only as far as wares are concerned. We ask extension to cover registration of shop cards, emblems and union services of whatever nature.
This request was repeated year after year by the same council when it appeared before members of the government. I quote also from a memorandum submitted to us by the All-Canadian Congress of Labour on January, 17, 1936. As regards this particular question it states:
Union Labels. While the union labels of organizations with headquarters in the United States are accepted by the customs authorities as evidence of the country of origin of merchandise imported into Canada, the amendment to the Trade Mark & Design Act in 1927 to permit the registration of union labels in Canada was virtually repealed by the Unfair Competition Act of 1932.
The new regulations under the act-both those directly prescribed by the law and those arbitrarily imposed by administrative order-[DOT] make registration futile, and they consequently operate to the detriment of Canadian unions. It is therefore requested that the right to make effective registration of union labels be restored by an amendment to the Unfair Competition Act.

I may say for the sake of correction that in the memorandum the Unfair Competition Act is not mentioned; it is the Copyright Act. That, however, is evidently a mistake. It has not seemed desirable nor even possible to amend the Unfair Competition Act to meet the wishes of these labour associations, but a separate bill altogether seems preferable.
I need not say any more than that the procedure which we have foreseen is similar in every respect to the one that obtained for the registration of trade marks proper. For the reasons I have indicated it will have to be distinct, but it will be similar, and registration will take place with the Department of the Secretary of State, although it is provided in the act that that may be changed [DOT] by order in council if that branch of the service should be later displaced.
When we are in committee and are considering these points one by one it will be possible to explain the bill further. Our only purpose is to meet the wishes of the labour unions and associations and to restore a condition that existed until 1932 and I believe was not done away with for any purpose except to have our trade mark act perfectly in accordance with the wishes expressed at the international conference at the Hague in 1925. Looking over the discussions which took place at the time I fail to see that there was the least desire to do away with the registration of shop cards, and I hope that this bill will meet with the approval of the house.

And so on. I think it is quite plain that it has always been so interpreted in the department, that that definition means an object. The only criticism I have, if it can be called a criticism, is that under the section of the Unfair Competition Act it says in respect of goods that they have been manufactured under a definite standard and definite working conditions. There were three definitions; first, of design mark, second, of word mark, and third, of trade mark. The word "trade mark" is defined by the statute as was read by the minister. "Design mark" is defined as follows:
(c) "Design mark" means a trade mark consisting of an arbitrary and in itself meaningless mark or design, or of a representation of some object or objects, or of letters or numerals in series or otherwise, or of a combination of two or more of the foregoing elements, and depending for its distinctiveness upon its form and colour, or upon the form, arrangement or colour of its several parts, independently of any idea or sound capable of being suggested by the particular sequence of the letters and/or numerals, if any, forming part thereof, or by their separation into groups, and includes any distinguishing guise capable of constituting a trade mark;
That is, capable of constituting it, of being made into a trade mark. Then there is a definition of "distinguishing guise", and lastly there is a definition of "word mark":
(o)	"Word mark" means a trade mark consisting only of a series of letters and/or numerals and depending for its distinctiveness upon the idea or sound suggested by the sequence of tile letters and/or numerals and their separation into groups, independently of the form of the letters or numerals severally or as a series.

stamp, ticket, device or other form of advertisement adopted by a labour union.
This is not a question of trade mark; it is a question of advertisement. I think the clause of the statute is broad enough, so far as the statute of 1932 is concerned, to permit of the registration of a design mark, but it is quite clear that this is not dealing with a trade mark, or design mark, or word mark. A shop card deals with only one thing-advertisement.
Paragraph (e) of subsection 2, which I am reading in connection with the definition, says that a shop card means any other form of advertising adopted by a labour union. This is the definition of an advertisement.

We must remember that we have an international convention on the word "trade mark" by which we are bound. The first conference took place in 1883. Then there was a revision in 1900, followed by the Washington conference of 1914 and the Hague conference of 1925.
The word "trade mark" as used in international law and as used by us now is defined by international agreement or understanding This is not a trade mark.

(1)	Upon the refusal of the registrar to grant, wholly or in part, any application authorized by this act to be made to him, the applicant may appeal from such refusal to the Exchequer Court of Canada within sixty days from the date upon which notice of the decision was despatched to him by the registrar or within such further time as the court may allow, either before or after the expiry of the sixty days aforesaid.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: This section provides a clarification of existing legislation. The clause amended has been rewritten because it gives rise to certain confusion in the minds of the officers who are administering it.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: There is no change, as I understand, in the amount of money to be collected?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: It is only a question of clarifying the conditions under which the payments shall be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext:
Exactly. Perhaps I had better explain paragraph (c). There is less

money to be collected; I do not want to lead my right hon. friend into error. Under the former act, under the definition of "vessel," a scow was included, but under this bill a scow which carries no crew will not have to pay sick mariners' fees.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: With regard to clause (b), will the minister explain wherein the amending clause changes the existing law?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: It really exempts certain ships. Owing to the definition of the word "voyage" which was contained in the old act, a vessel coming to Canada and unloading its cargo at, let us say, Three Rivers, finishing its voyage at that place and then going on to Montreal to take on a new cargo and start a new voyage, would have been obliged to pay dues twice. Now it will be considered that the term "voyage" will cover not only the discharging of the cargo at Three Rivers, but the taking on of a new cargo at Montreal.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: A ship pays once with respect to each arrival in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: That is all very well with regard to a ship that is on schedule. But if the minister will look at the amendment he will find it imposes this obligation, that the ship "is returning or proceeding immediately to a place out of Canada." The old act reads that "the ship is a ship which came from a place out of Canada and has paid dues on the same voyage in a previous port of call in Canada." Suppose a ship returns to Canada and comes to Halifax. She unloads part of her cargo and goes to Lunenburg. She is not on schedule, but is laid up, looking for cargo; that vessel must pay a second time according to the amendment, although *under the old law she would not have to pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: She would not pay a second time unless she started a new voyage. She would not pay again if she went to Lunenburg to lay up.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: I think so. "A ship which came from and is returning or proceeding immediately to a place out of Canada." A ship is not returning to a place out of Canada unless she has a charter party or is on schedule. The example I have suggested is that of a ship which returns to Canada, comes to a home port, and may be laid up in port, and for that reason is obliged to pay dues the second time.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. member's interpretation is correct. If the ship came to Lunenburg and from there proceeded to engage in the coasting trade, mariners' dues would be exacted. That, I believe, has

Shipping Act-Marine Hospitals
been the custom; perhaps it will be clearer under the present legislation. If a vessel comes from a transatlantic port to Canada, and, finishing its voyage in Canada, discharging its cargo, undertakes to engage in the coasting trade, even though it remains in the same province and goes from Halifax to Lunenburg, Lunenburg to Sydney, etc., it will pay duty three times during the one season. But that is the present custom; there is no change so far as that is concerned. The object of this amendment is to exempt certain vessels from this duty, not to increase its application.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: I am glad to hear the minister's explanation; that is what I am really interested in. But I am bound to say that this underlined portion which states "a ship wrhich came from and is returning or proceeding immediately to a place out of Canada" does, it seems to me, impose a responsibility on the ship of proceeding on another foreign voyage immediately, and if the vessel is out of charter or is not on schedule it seems to me she is obligated to pay dues a second time.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: Unless the ship was engaged in trading in the second port she would not be obliged to.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: It is all right, if you say that.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: The difficulty of the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg is with the word "immediately." The case as put is this. A ship comes from Liverpool to Lunenburg, and if she returns from Lunenburg to Southampton, she has paid dues once and that is the end of it. If, leaving Lunenburg, she goes down to Shelburne and proceeds abroad from there, it is understood she pays dues only once, and this is to protect her against having to pay them twice. I apprehend that the difficulty-and I think there is some force in the point made by the hon. member-is in the word "immediately," because it is said that the ship has now come from Liverpool to Lunenburg and she returns to Southampton, a port out of Canada, or she proceeds "immediately" to a place out of Canada: the proceeding "immediately" to a place out of Canada does make it a little difficult.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: But no vessels pay duty when they proceed from one port within a province to another port within a province unless they are engaged in the coasting trade.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext:
Quite. There is no doubt about that. I was thinking of some form of words other than "immediately."

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext:
The following words
qualify it.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: Supposing the ship to which the leader of the opposition has referred were to be laid up in Halifax for six months and then go out to Southampton, would she have to pay twice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: No; she has paid duty "since arrival in a previous port of call in Canada."

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext:
The previous section
deals entirely with coasting trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext:
Perhaps I may make it clear if I explain to the committee just what vessels do pay and when they pay.
1.	Compulsory payment by vessels from foreign ports entering maritime ports of Canada and ports in Manitoba and Ontario on Hudson and James bay.
2.	All vessels engaged in the coasting trade of Canada which ply between maritime provinces.
3.	All vessels engaged in the coasting trade of Canada which have made one payment. A vessel must complete the three payments at the next two succeeding ports if it is engaged in the coasting trade.
Of course, all hon. members who have any knowledge of the maritime provinces know that fishing vessels may pay prior to undertaking the first fishing voyage of the calendar year, provided they are registered.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: And get the benefit.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: If a vessel, coming from outside Canada, calls at Yarmouth, say, for the purpose of discharging cargo or in order to get away from the weather, and then goes to Lunenburg, payment is made at Yarmouth and she is exempt when she goes to Lunenburg. Under the new law, if she goes to Lunenburg and proceeds immediately to a place outside Canada she does not have to pay, but if that condition does not exist she does have to pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: The qualifying words follow. She has paid a duty since arrival in a previous port of call.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext:
Yes, she paid when she came to Yarmouth; but when she goes to Lunenburg the customs officer demands payment again. If the ship is leaving Canada immediately the ship is exempt; otherwise it must pay.

Narcotic Drug Act

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 SICK MARINERS AND MARINE HOSPITALS-LEVY, COLLECTION AND REMISSION OF 8HIP DUES
speechtext: No, because she would not be engaged in the coasting trade of Canada. Under subsection 12 of section 2 of the act, the coasting trade of Canada includes carriage by water of goods or passengers from one port or place in Canada to another. In the instance the hon. gentleman has mentioned by way of illustration, the vessel is not carrying goods or passengers from one port or place to another, but is simply calling at a port for the purpose of laying up.

speechtext:

Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of Pensions and National Health) moved the second reading of Bill No. 24, to amend the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, 1929.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston (Lake Centre) in the chair.
On section 1-Licences.

This section refers to production, and I suppose that means of opium or any other narcotic drug or any weed, for instance, which may be grown in Canada. I have heard a rumour that some such weed is being grown in this country and is being used in the form of cigarettes which have a more or less harmful effect. I have been told also that the experimental farm is engaged in some production along that line. I do not know whether it is so, but the minister will no doubt be able to inform us. If a weed of this kind is being grown in Canada there must be some source from which the seeds are obtained and a record of the extent of land under cultivation. Can the minister give us any information as to how much of this weed is being produced and what it is being used for?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
This particular section refers to the production of any drug; but since the proposed amendments deal to a considerable extent with the attempt which is being made by the department to control what, though it cannot be called a new drug, is a new menace to the youth of the country, perhaps I had

better make some observations with respect to the weed that is known as marihuana. This is by no means a new drug; it was known as far back as the days of Homer.
Is that the reason Homer nodded?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No; on the contrary, the effect is not to make people nod; it is exceedingly stimulating. It is probably the reason why there was an attack on Troy.
Is its production a new thing in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Perhaps it might be well to give an idea what it is. In the old days it was known as hashish, and it has a dozen different names throughout the East. Our modern word " assassin " comes from the name given to the people who were first known to have used it, the assassins, in the early days of Christianity, and the use of the drug has spread throughout the world, the eastern world particularly. It came to us through the United States from Mexico, where it is known as marihuana. It is known scientifically under the name of cannabis sativa. It grows wild in certain countries, generally speaking in temperate climates. It is used in windbreaks in western Canada, the leaves being the portion which, when made into something resembling tobacco, is extremely dangerous if smoked. It is made into cigarettes that resemble tobacco cigarettes and is peddled around largely to the youth of the country. The United States government has taken an extremely serious view of it, and is now endeavouring by federal legislation to control its cultivation, manufacture and sale.
In these amendments we are asking that the production and also the cultivation be prohibited. My hon. friend asked if there had been any cultivation in Canada. I find there has been no cultivation for commercial purposes, although it is grown at Emerson, Manitoba, and was found on a vacant lot in Calgary. Certain of our European immigrants have been using it for extracting an oil to be used as a substitute for fat. There was a certain area cropped at the central experimental farm in Ottawa, and another area at a substation near Montreal.

Will the minister tell
us to what extent it has been used in Canada to the knowledge of the department, as an illicit drug?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
My information is that since 1932 we have had twenty-eight convictions for the possession of this drug. But the im-

Narcotic Drug Act
portance of endeavouring to control it is that it is about the only habit forming drug which is produced in Canada. In any other case our efforts are confined to keeping the drug out of Canada; but here is something growing right in our own country, and it is extremely difficult to control unless authority is given to the department to control the production and cultivation also.
The word "production" necessarily conveys the idea that it is being produced in Canada. I was wondering to what extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Up to the present time that used in the traffic has. as far as we know, been imported. It usually crosses the border through Windsor. But there is nothing to prevent anybody from going into the business here.
This is a sort of preventive measure.

The purpose of the legislation is, I understand, to control the production of this extremely deleterious drug. While control of production may have far-reaching effects and do a great deal of good, I should like to ask the minister whether any attempt is being made or contemplated to eradicate the plant as a weed. It appears to me we shall not achieve the purpose for which this legislation is intended if we control only the production, while at the same time the plant from which the drug is made grows wild as a weed and may be gathered by those who recognize it and make it into tobacco form.

Under section 3 of the bill
we are taking power to control the cultivation and also the gathering and production. We are endeavouring to find out where it grows. So far we have located it in certain parts of Canada, and I suppose by education we shall try to impress on the people of Canada the evil results from its use. Once we have this authority, whenever we find it we shall be able to prevent the cultivation of it.

Does the bill make provision for a penalty for those having it in their
possession?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is already in the act.

Are there any good purposes to which this weed can be put? I am very much interested in the minister's remarks. I happened to read the other day a report of H. F. Anslinger, United States Commissioner of Narcotics; he calls this drug the assassin of youth, and states that it is one of the greatest menaces which has ever struck that country. It seems to me that very severe penalties should be imposed for the
production or sale of this drug. The eradication of it is certainly necessary. If there are no good purposes to which it can be put, I do not see why licences should be granted; rather steps should be taken to eradicate it entirely, because it is something that could undermine the youth of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The penalty is fairly severe, seven years' imprisonment and the lash. With respect to uses to which it can be put, I have before me extracts from the evidence given at the sittings of the committee of the house of representatives at Washington. It says:
Hemp is cultivated for three purposes, (1) for the fibre, out of which rope, twine, cloth and hats are made, (2) for the seed, from which a rapidly drying oil is obtained as a commercial substitute for linseed oil, and (3) for the narcotic contained in the resin of the dried flowering tops of the pistillate plant. The seed is also sold as a constituent of commercial bird seed.
I want to make a distinction between these two, the hemp plant and the plant that provides the fibre for rope making. There is no connection whatever. All our ropes are made from hard fibres and have been ever since the sixties. These fibres are produced only in the tropics, while the hemp plant that produces soft fibre or the marihuana occurs only in temperate climates for fibre production. Marihuana hemp is used for commercial twines, such as bookbinders twine, hatters twine for sewing hats, and it was formerly used for what was called express twine or heavy twine.

I hoped that the minister would say that he would prohibit the production for commercial purposes, not issue a licence. To issue a licence involves recognition of the production. In view of the very serious situation to which attention has been directed, I think the proper course would be that the minister be authorized to take steps to prohibit production in commercial quantities. I do not think we could contemplate its production at all if it is half as bad as has been stated. I do not believe the situation is very bad yet in this country but certainly the reports indicate that it is very serious in the United States. If that report of the investigation is to be taken as a correct statement, should we not face the problem at once and say that we shall eradicate its production for commercial purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
There is some difficulty. Since the bill was introduced I have been informed that in certain sections of the country some farmers had gone in for the cultivation of this plant, and in fact, as my right hon. friend knows, during the war the Canadian government at the instance of the British government actually encouraged the growing of hemp, and though I understand it was not successfully grown in this country, whatever
Narcotic Drug Act

was grown was not used in the making of rope or twine. I am informed that far the greater part went into upholstery, and a great deal was wasted. But the fact remains that we have in this country, I am informed, a number of farmers who have gone into the cultivation of this and have bought machinery to gather it, and perhaps some hardship would be caused to them if growing it were prohibited. But it is the intention of the department, unless very strong reason is shown, not to issue any licences.

I thought the minister would say that it was not proposed to issue licences. But with great respect I say that begs the question of the destruction of the plant and the prohibition of its production for commercial purposes.

How is the United States handling the situation? In the report I have before me I note that in New York state, for instance, 200 acres of growing plants were destroyed by the authorities. In Louisiana the officials made a raid in which 500,000 plants were destroyed. It seems to me that evidently they are trying to eradicate the plant altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: In the United States they have a provision similar to this one. They found that it was impossible to enforce total prohibition at once, but they are administering by means of licences. I may say the bill came into force only on October 1, 1937. The latest reports I have from the United States are to the effect that total seizures of marihuana in that country during 1937 amounted to 98,000 pounds of growing plants and 667 pounds of bulk marihuana. This was taken from 1,909 acres. Between October 1, 1937, when the United States federal law came into effect, and December 31 of that year, seizures by federal officials involved 1,000 pounds of growing plants and 452 pounds of bulk marihuana.
Of growing plants?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes.
A thousand pounds?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes.
It must have been a hundred tons.
No; there are only forty-nine tons altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is in the three months since October 1.
The plants are being seized?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes, they are seizing the plants.
We could not seize them.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: But we will, under the section.
Is the same drug extracted from hemp? It seems to me that the experimental farm officials have announced that that is so.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The experimental farm has been growing the plant for the stalk. The stalk is innocuous, but the flowering tops and the leaves are dangerous. In that state they sell for as much as S20 per pound. I have no doubt it would be possible to control cultivation, even under another government.
But is not this weed or drug extracted from hemp?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The plant itself is known as hemp. As I understand it, the process is not complicated. The leaves are simply chopped and made into a kind of tobacco, which is dried. That is all there is to it, unless there is some process of extraction, with which I am not familiar, to make it still stronger. But it can be used as a habit forming drug by simply drying and powdering the leaves.
What does the experimental farm do with the leaves it produces?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: This year they were left on the ground and ploughed in. The marihuana menace has been drawn to the attention of the people in Canada and the United States only within the last three or four years, so that I would not be at all surprised if large numbers of people were unwittingly growing the plant -and in that I would include perhaps some government departments.

Is it the purpose of the government not only to curtail but to eradicate altogether the production of the drug? I am convinced that anything which can be misused to break down our manhood should be investigated. The farmer producing the plant should be compensated, and the plant eliminated.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I can give the committee
the undertaking that no licence will be issued until we have a complete survey of the localities in which the plant is grown, and to what use it would be put. Our hope is that within a short time it will be possible absolutely to prohibit cultivation and production, as well as sale and manufacture.

Narcotic Drug Act
What steps have been taken in the United States to eradicate the plant as a weed?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The United States have passed a bill, in somewhat similar terms, which came into effect on October 1, 1937.
What practical steps have been taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Within the last two or three months, and during the course of 1937, certain seizures in plant and bulk form have been made.

Probably I have not made myself clear. Apparently the plant grows as a weed. The minister has told us that it was found in a vacant lot in Calgary, and in other parts of western Canada. What steps have been taken by the government to locate it, where it is grown innocently? Have the United States government taken steps to locate where it is grown in that way?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I am informed that on account of the difficulty of running this thing down in the United States, that has not been done completely. The act has been in force only since last October. They have not yet reached the point where they can say just where the plant is grown, in what quantities it is grown or how they are going to proceed to eradicate it. I may add, however, that I believe over forty states of the union have passed legislation with respect to marihuana. It was found advisable, nevertheless, to have some measure of federal control.

Because the weed is not generally known or recognized, and because its use is so harmful, I would suggest that the government, through its publicity branch and educational features, should bring to the attention of the people of Canada the fact that the weed has far-reaching, poisonous and demoralizing effects. I believe along that line something could be done which would be of greater value than any attempt to stop production.
While I am in favour of stopping production and the use of the weed as a drug, or in the form of cigarettes, before too many lives are endangered, before the morals of the people are contaminated and before the drug comes into general use, however unwittingly on the part of the public, I say the department might well take into consideration the issuance of educational circulars dealing with its deleterious effects.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I should be glad to take that into consideration. The only thing which
prevents me from saying at once that we shall proceed with an educational campaign is the fear that it might advertise the use of the drug. If it is at all possible to proceed educationally without, at the same time, telling the people where they can get it and how they can use it, I should be very glad to follow the hon. member's suggestion.

It seems to me that the harships endured by any farmers who may have equipped themselves to produce this plant are of very slight importance as compared with the evil effects that the continuance of the growing of the plant would have. The results of the use of it have been proved to be serious. Many municipalities are equipped with inexpensive spraying equipment which could be used in the eradication of the plant wherever it is found growing as a weed. I suggest that the department consult with the municipalities regarding the spraying of this weed wherever it is found.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I am informed that we are pretty well ahead of the problem in Canada. In the United States the problem overtook them before they were ready, in that the use of this drug grew up with amazing rapidity So far in Canada we have not had that to contend with. Our trouble at the present time is the imported drug. So far as we know there has been no use for drug addiction purposes of any of the plants grown in Canada. I think I can give assurance that there is no intention to issue licences; but before we take any drastic steps I think we should know just where the plant is being cultivated, the extent of its cultivation and whether any interest will be injuriously affected by an immediate prohibition. It may be that someone, unknowingly and without malice, has invested a fairly substantial amount of money in preparing for the cultivation of this plant. If so, he will be advised that we shall not permit this cultivation. I think that is all we can do for the moment.

In many parts of western Canada this weed is grown as a windbreak around the gardens, but most of the English speaking people do not realize to what grave uses it could be put. If this matter is advertised they will realize to what uses people put this plant. I think it would be wiser for the government to cooperate with the municipalities and the provinces in eradication work. You can go for 800 miles or so through the west and in probably every other garden you will find this weed. I do not think its use should be advertised. The
Narcotic Drug Act

government should work in secret with the provinces and the municipalities to eradicate this weed. As I say, it is used as a windbreak and in some cases as tobacco.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2, 3 and 4 agreed to.
On section 5-Burden of proof.

At first glance this
section would seem to be unfair. The minister has stated that this marihuana grows wild as a weed in many places, but I notice that the section reads:
Without limiting the generality of paragraph (d) of section four of this act, any person who occupies, controls, or is in possession of any building, room, vessel, vehicle, enclosure or place, in or upon which any drug or article mentioned in section II is found, shall, if charged with having such drug or article in possession without lawful authority, be deemed to have been so in possession unless he prove that the drug or article was there without his authority, knowledge or consent, or that he was lawfully entitled to the possession thereof.
It is quite possible that an individual might not know that this weed was growing wild on his land and under this section he might be put to an expense which he should not have to incur. I think the minister will agree with me that it might not be the fault of an individual if a weed was growing wild on his land.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Section 17 does not refer only to marihuana; it refers to all drugs. There is a section in the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act which places the burden of proof that he is not unlawfully in possession upon the person who has the drug. The only purpose of the amendment is to add the words * or article mentioned in section eleven." That would refer to articles such as opium pipes, utensils for cooking opium or things of that kind. It has no direct reference to marihuana; and even if this amended section did not pass, the act with respect to other drugs would remain the same.
It would have no particular reference to a weed growing on a person's land?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No.

Subsection 5 states that a person charged with having such drug or article in his possession without lawful authority, shall "be deemed to have been so in possession unless he prove that the drug or article was there without his authority, knowledge or consent, or that he was lawfully entitled to the possession thereof." I submit that the narcotic drug control exercised by the government in past years has fallen far

short of what it should he. Reference has been made to marihuana, but we should not forget that this act covers all narcotic drugs. Wholesale drug houses throughout Canada are permitted to keep large stocks of opium and other narcotic drugs on hand, and I should like to know what control is exercised by the government over these supplies. I could take up considerable time in discussing this question, but I shall not. A word to the wise should be sufficient. Mention has been made of the great number of motor accidents these days, and when one's attention is called to this one invariably thinks of the narcotic addicts who might be at the steering wheels of motor cars. These wholesale drug houses have branches in many of the provinces, and quite often the branches are in charge of people who have not the pharmaceutical knowledge to see that the drugs in their care are distributed in the proper manner. These branches may have in their custody just as large supplies of these drugs as the head office may desire them to have. There does not seem to be any supervision by the government in this connection.
One could not help being struck by the words of the Prime Minister of Great Britain when, speaking with reference to the resignation of Mr. Anthony Eden, he referred to the sham of the League of Nations at Geneva. The very same thing has been evidenced here year after year. I mentioned it the year before last, and to-day it is more apparent than ever. We have been sending men from the narcotic drugs branch over to Geneva on joy rides, at the expense of the Canadian people, and what ever came of it? Was codeine banned? They discussed it for years at Geneva, and yet to-day codeine is sold in Canada holus-bolus over the counter to every man, woman or child who wants to purchase it. The purchasers take it, get in their cars and drive over the highways, and lives are lost. Codeine has never been counted as a narcotic by Canada, but it was banned as a narcotic by the United States government unhesitatingly, without regard to the League of Nations. Yet Canada cannot see her way to stopping the sale of codeine to our people. This act contemplates putting it under control; I am well aware of that; but if there is no more control than there has been in the past of codeine and other narcotic drugs, if there is no better administration of the act, we are wasting our time here and deluding the people of the country into the belief that we are protecting them from the effects of narcotics.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
With respect to the observations of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Hartigan), the importation of

Narcotic Drug Act
narcotics generally-and the question really resolves itself into a question of importation- is perhaps more rigidly controlled than he would seem to indicate. No one can bring into this country' any such drug as opium or morphine or heroin without first obtaining a licence. Then the drug has to be brought in through the customs ports, where all drug importations are carefully checked. Then it goes to the wholesalers, whose supplies are constantly checked by the inspectors of the department. The wholesalers, if they open a branch, must obtain a licence also for the branch. When the drug goes from the wholesaler or distributor or branch into individual drug stores or into the hands of private practitioners, a register must be kept and a check is made even of the supplies which have been delivered to the physician, and if it is found that there has been an excessive or abnormal delivery to any physician the department gets into touch with him and endeavours to ascertain just why this abnormal condition exists.
With respect to codeine, my hon. friend has on a number of occasions drawn to my attention his views regarding this drug. The League of Nations, at their meetings, have decided that codeine is not the kind of drug which must be subjected within the country where it is sold to the same restrictions as some other drugs; but internationally it is subject to some control of movement between countries. Within our own country we have arrived at this arrangement:	In four provinces codeine is subject to the same or somewhat similar regulation as other drugs, under provincial legislation; and in all the provinces, by arrangement between the federal government and the pharmaceutical associations with the assistance of the narcotic drug wholesalers, we have put into effect a plan which limits drug store purchases to actual medical needs. A maximum purchase of one ounce monthly was put into effect in 1935.

May I ask which are the
four provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario.
Does the minister mean one ounce monthly per patient or per drug store ?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Per drug store.

Does the department
consider that that arrangement has been kept by the wholesalers in their deliveries of codeine? You will find more than an ounce of codeine in a bottle of 222's or in any other form of codeine tablets. There is an eighth of a grain of codeine in each tablet.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
My information is that
under this voluntary arrangement the drug stores are not able to get more than one ounce monthly, and of course their sales are registered, so they cannot sell more than the one ounce.

I think that the handling
of the narcotic drug trade in Canada is very well done. Speaking from personal observation I have always considered that the officials were doing good work, but I am inclined to agree that codeine is not handled in Canada as it should be. It should not be allowed to enter or to be sold in this country. The minister has just told me that Saskatchewan is one of the four provinces which have certain regulations regarding the sale of codeine. I know for a fact that you can purchase 222's, containing codeine, the drug mentioned by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Hartigan). without any restrictions whatever on the sale. I am firmly convinced, in spite of what many men who should know a good deal about it say, that codeine is a habit forming drug; I am satisfied of that. If that is true, I am equally satisfied that something more should be done in Canada than has been done to prevent any habit forming drug from being distributed in the way codeine is allowed to be at present.

I should like to congratulate
the minister on this bill. I think it is very necessary for us to curtail the sale of codeine. It is possible that orientals bootleg this stuff into Canada more than we realize. In regard to hemp, I believe they are in the habit of using the leaves of the hemp on the sly, and it is very much to the advantage of this country that we should have an act such as this in force. I believe that a good many accidents on the highway, more than we would think from the reports, are due to liquor. In the old country they report that fifty per cent of their highway accidents are due to liquor. Personally I believe that many of our highway accidents are due to people smoking cigarettes with dope in them. After the driver has smoked a few he becomes addicted to them, and soon he is not watching his car as he should be doing. I think it will mean much to have this act in force.

Section agreed to.
On section 6-Additions to schedule.

This section is one giving very wide powers to the governor in council. It authorizes the transfer of preparations from one category to another at the instance of the government, which in times past would have been regarded by the minister as so ter-
Narcotic Drug Act

rible a thing to do as almost to invite an earthquake. It seems to me an extensive grant of power to one man.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I am inclined to agree with my right hon. friend, but the situation which arises would be this. Let us suppose that at the League of Nations meeting at Geneva it is decided that codeine should be in a certain category; in order to enable the minister to cany out the arrangements at Geneva a whole year must elapse. The purpose of the amendment is really to cover that situation.

So far as that phase of the matter is concerned I think that is desirable, but there should be added to it that it be published in the Canada Gazette immediately thereafter. It might be put in three or four years afterwards.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The amendment provides that " every order in council made in that behalf shall be published in the Canada Gazette "-
Yes, I see that, but it does not say when.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: -[DOT]" and shall take effect at the expiration of thirty days from the date of such publication.'' It will not be in effect until thirty days after it is published.
Quite. But the order in council might be passed and publication might not take place for two or three months.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: But it would not be of any use to the minister or administration-

I agree with that, but it is desirable it should be. That is the point I was making. If it is desirable to pass it at all, it should become effective without delay. Perhaps Mr. O'Connor will deal with that.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-Application of certain sections of the act.

In regard to this section there is a point that the department would be well advised to bear in mind, and that is with regard to the present administrators of the act. While the wording is all right and the intention of the government is no doubt good, it can be readily understood that difficulty arises when it is left to a body of mounted policemen to go into the drug stores and check the receipts and outgoings of any narcotic. You cannot take haphazard a body of that kind and entrust it with such work. I have seen some of these men go into a drug store and try to check it over; I am not

casting any reflection on the mounted police as a body or, as far as that goes, on any particular individual in it, but I say that they are not the right body to be entrusted with the checking of sales of drugs in the drug stores of the dominion. It is almost like a bull in a china cabinet; it is just antagonizing the people who are in the drug business, because it leaves the impression that they may be guilty of some offence. If any customer happens to be in the store when the officer comes in, the first thought in that customer's mind will be, "This drug store must be in bad repute with the department when they have to send a policeman down here and take the manager into an inside office to check over his books and accounts." That has happened on more than one occasion. On other occasions the findings on the check-up have been far different from those reported to the heads of the department at Ottawa; of this I have very definite proof, and I am prepared to put it forward at any time it is requested. The check-up system in respect of narcotics should be changed.

In my opinion, as one who has had some experience in the drug business, the sale of narcotic drugs is very carefully supervised by the department. In order to buy a narcotic the druggist must send an order certifying the amount; that amount is supplied to the store upon that order; if the druggist has two or three stores he may not transfer narcotics from one to the other; each store must stand on its own order in that regard. The druggist must keep a register, and in it he must keep the amount balanced as between his sales and his purchases; a mounted police officer comes in, usually once a month, and checks that record. I do not know of any more efficient control or any better type of inspector that could be obtained within the community for the purpose of the inspection of these books than the mounted police officer. He does it well; he does it without offence, and he does it with a certain prestige behind him which is derived from the organization he represents. I realize that the sale of narcotics is a serious matter, but they may be sold only upon the prescription of a doctor. It seems to me that, at least in the part of the country from which I come, there is no great trouble with regard to the act; it is not being violated, and everybody is trying to observe it in the best way possible.

Section agreed to.
Sections 8 to 10 inclusive agreed to.
May I suggest to the minister that it might be desirable to con-

Narcotic Drug Act
sider whether this act should come into force at a date to be named? If it were to come into force at once upon receiving the royal assent, it might cause some difficulties with respect to those who are not informed as to its terms; I refer to the early part of the act. Would it not be desirable that it shall come into force by proclamation or upon a date to be fixed? I recall that in 1932 when we were passing a certain act we thought it desirable to do this, for the reasons I have indicated. I do not know whether they apply with equal force to this measure; but it occurred to me that they might, having regard to some of the provisions we have dealt with this afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: In 1932, as I am informed, the reason the difficulty arose was that there was an international convention-
Quite.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: -and the endeavour was to bring the act into effect at the same time as the convention. As a matter of fact there is a convention covering quite a number of the amendments submitted, and so far it has not been ratified by the house.

The fact that the bill has been introduced led me to assume that that was not necessary, because I recall vividly that many of the matters we have dealt with were discussed at the international convention at Geneva. I think it well to say that most Canadians are proud of the part taken at these international conventions by Colonel Sharman, who is here this afternoon; he has made a real contribution to the work of the conventions; I think that is admitted by all who have had to do with them.
I should like to identify myself with what has been said by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley) as to the method of enforcement of the act. What that hon. member has said is wholly in accordance with what I have observed, at any rate in western Canada, that the police usually go in after hours or at a time convenient to the druggist, look at the ledger and take particulars of the sales he has made to make sure that they balance with the receipts of narcotics during the previous month. Some druggists complain that it is difficult to get supplies, because of the severity with which the audit is carried on.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I shall be glad to accept the suggestion of the right hon. gentleman and allow this bill to stand in order to consider adding such a clause.
The minister can look into the matter. I do not know that it is necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not know whether it is necessary or not.
The reason it may be necessary is that the house has not yet ratified certain conventions upon which uniform action was predicated by various countries of the world.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: But there is no urgency as to that.

I should like to call the minister's attention to section 9, although it has been passed. I was wondering why the words "except the seed" were put in. In western Canada poppy seeds are used to a considerable extent, being ground up and used in bread by eastern Europeans. In my opinion the control of the poppy should be brought to the attention of the minister particularly at this time, because the use of it in the way I have described is harmful to young and growing people. The older people use it in bread, for what purpose I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My hon. friend will note that the seed is excepted from the terms of the act and he will also observe that we describe a certain kind of poppy.
We do not grow the opium poppy in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I think we do, in some of the western states.
Not western "states" yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
It is grown in British Columbia. I am informed that the oriental population grow it for the sake of a sort of narcotic beverage which is obtained by boiling down the heads. They get a kind of tea which has certain narcotic qualities.
Progress reported.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO STATUTORY GRADES OF WESTERN GRAIN

speechtext:
Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 27, to amend the Canada Grain Act.
He said: While it is my intention to request that the bill be referred to the committee on agriculture after it has received the second reading, perhaps I might make a few comments upon what is proposed in it.
7S0
Grain Act-Statutory Grades

Briefly, it provides for the exclusion of garnet wheat from grades 3 and 4 Manitoba northern. As hon. members know, it is already excluded from the higher grade. The bill also provides for the establishing of three grades of garnet; we shall have three grades of garnet. It provides further that there shall be no mixing in grades 1 and 2 of garnet wheat, and that anything which does not qualify for the three grades of garnet shall be put into the commercial grades of red spring wheat. One other provision is that in these garnet grades 1 and 2 any overages exceeding one-quarter of one per cent shall belong to the crown.
That, briefly, is all that is contained in the bill. I do not know whether the house would care to discuss the matter now, but it seemed to me that inasmuch as there are very many members who have no particular interest in wheat, it would be well to refer the bill to the standing committee on agriculture.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO STATUTORY GRADES OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: I submit that this bill should not be introduced until after the Turgeon report is presented.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO STATUTORY GRADES OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: It was introduced yesterday.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO STATUTORY GRADES OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: But it should not be proceeded with until after that report is presented. If that report is of the importance indicated; if it deals with garnet wheat as it is said it does, surely the house is entitled to the benefit of that knowledge before it gives second reading to the bill.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO STATUTORY GRADES OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: I might say in reply to my right hon. friend something which perhaps will satisfy him. Before the bill was introduced; before it was framed-and it was framed b3' the board of grain commissioners with the support of most of the interested parties-I took advantage of an opportunity to discuss it with the commissioner, Judge Turgeon.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO STATUTORY GRADES OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: That makes it just that much worse.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO STATUTORY GRADES OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: I was i.fraid it would not satisfy my right hon. friend.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO STATUTORY GRADES OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman must realize that not only is an ex parte conversation with a commissioner bad, but to come into the house and say that he has had that conversation, and based legislation upon it, is worse still.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO STATUTORY GRADES OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: I did not even tell my right hon. friend what the result of my conversation was.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO STATUTORY GRADES OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: You did not have to, because you should not be talking to him at all about it.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO STATUTORY GRADES OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: I shall have to take issue with my right hon. friend.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO STATUTORY GRADES OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: You can take issue.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO STATUTORY GRADES OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: However, the matter stands just as I have stated it. If the house does not choose to give the bill its second reading, that is, of course, the privilege of the house. I think that the public interest would be properly served if the bill were given second reading and then referred to the committee on agriculture, where all those in favour of or opposed to it can make representations and arrive at some decision which will be acceptable to the house.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO STATUTORY GRADES OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: From what the minister has said, I am in agreement with the principle of the bill as he has outlined it, and it may be all right for it to go to the committee. As regards what the Turgeon commission may report, that is another matter altogether. I wonder whether it would be out of order for me to ask the minister at this stage when we may expect the report from the Turgeon commission. Shall we get it during the present session, and if so, how soon?

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO STATUTORY GRADES OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: Possibly I should mention another matter, one of the reasons why the bill is introduced now. It is important, I believe, that the grain growers of western Canada should have knowledge as to what it is proposed to do with garnet. It may affect their seeding of garnet wheat. The complete report of Judge Turgeon will be presented before the session is over, though I am not in a position at the moment to say how soon. I do not think the report will be unduly delayed, but before it is received it is well that the grain growers of western Canada should know exactly what we propose to do with respect to garnet, and that is a reason why this bill precedes the general amending of the grain act which will follow after the Turgeon report is received. That, I believe, is a sufficient reason why the house should enact the present amendment.

Would the minister say whether this equipment has been increased since the administration of the harbours has been placed under the Department of Transport, whether any equipment has been sold, or the quantity increased, and whether the amount of equipment and number of vessels used now are greater or less than when the administration was taken over from the commissions?

As far as the harbour
commissions are concerned, the equipment is less. The principal change is in Montreal harbour, where we had quite a number of units that had been more or less laid up for several years. We had two small tugs there, used intermittently, but a number of units at Montreal harbour were sold when the St. Lawrence dredging fleet was sold. In addition we have sold two small buoy service vessels and one old icebreaker on the St. Lawrence. We refitted one of the coal barges to do buoy work on the Pacific and one on the Pacific coast has been sold. We are reducing our fleet and trying to operate the service with fewer boats and with more efficient equipment.
My next question is, Which ones have been sold, how sold, whether by tender or how, and who were the purchasers?

The Mikula, an ice-breaker, the Loos, which was a service boat, the Gulnare, which is a service boat, and the Newington, a buoy service boat working out of Prince Rupert, were sold through the salvage board. The remainder, that is the dredging fleet on the St. Lawrence and the surplus equipment in Montreal harbour, were sold in one lot by negotiated agreement.
Sold through the salvage commission, or is it just one officer, the salvage officer?

We call it the salvage board. There was a salvage officer who died a few months ago, but I think Mr. Watson Sellar, Comptroller of the Treasury, is really the officer of the government who represents the salvage board.

All right.

Under what item does the minister propose to discuss the disposal of the St. Lawrence dredging fleet and things of that kind?

The other day I had a question on the order paper, which was answered, but I should like to get some further information. The Collingwood boat went on hydrographic survey, I think?

I asked the speed and the consumption of coal. I was told that the speed was between six and a half and seven and a half knots an hour and the coal consumption thirteen and a half tons for twenty-four hours. That is not thirteen and a half tons per hour, is it?

A rather low fuel consumption. What is the size of the boat?

About 150 feet. The slow speed helps the fuel consumption, of course. We are putting new propellers on it .this spring, which will bring the speed up to about eight and a half knots, which we think is enough.

Would the minister give the committee information with regard to the feeder services to the Trans-Canada service. I
had the pleasure of taking some part in the opening of the airport last summer at Oliver which, as the minister knows, is an admirably developed airport. It is the point on the Trans-Canada service where it crosses the Okanagan valley which runs north from the centre of the state of Washington, up to the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway. What possibility is there in the near future of developing a feeder service in that valley. There are several other localities in southern British Columbia which require facilities for moving freight, passengers and perhaps mail.

The Trans-Canada Air Lines are confining themselves to through services, from "Vancouver to the maritime provinces, the only deviation from that being the line from Lethbridge to Edmonton, the capital city of Alberta, and such international services as may later be decided upon as a logical part of that operation.
It is intended that the feeder services will be left to private enterprise, under arrangement with the Post Office Department. The post office requirement will largely determine the number of feeder services to be inaugurated. At this time tenders are being called for a service connecting the principal cities in Saskatchewan with the Trans-Canada at Regina. I am sure that later on other services will be developed westerly from that point. Of course the Post Office Department's requirements are something outside the province of the Department of Transport, and I should have to take the matter up with the Post Office Department before I could answer the hon. member with respect to the possibility of a route in the Okanagan valley. I believe I can say that it is the intention to extend as rapidly as possible aviation to the principal centres in Oanada, wiherever postal traffic will warrant.

The minister was' good enough this summer to visit Windsor. His assurances in connection with the place the city of Windsor would occupy in the province of aerial navigation in Canada were indeed encouraging. I am wondering if he would care to make a statement with regard to the position of Windsor, not as a point on the main line, but largely because of its accessibility to the United States in a direct line from Toronto to Windsor and Chicago.

It is rather early to speak definitely about the route from Toronto, west. It is the intention, of course, to establish a connection west from Toronto with either Chicago or Detroit. So far as I know, the
Supply-Transport-Aviation

department has plans for Windsor, but unfortunately we have not had very much cooperation from that city. We look for some help from the cities by way of furnishing air fields. At this time the whole situation in so far as Windsor is concerned is a little indefinite. We hope to make some progress this year in that particular direction.
What plans has the department in mind for Calgary?

The situation in Calgary is still being explored. The field previously used is not adequate for high speed equipment. It can be used in favourable weather. We hope to obtain a better field there shortly. We are prepared to cooperate with the city, but unfortunately the city is not in a position at this time to cooperate with us. So there qgain it is a little premature to say what eventually the solution of the Calgary situation will be. It is one of two or three spots in Canada the plans for which have not yet been completely worked out.
What is the situation with reference to the extension of service to the maritime provinces? What will be the terminus there and what feeder lines are contemplated?

The situation in the maritime provinces has not been worked out in detail. As the hon. member knows, the route has been developed from the westerly end and we have completed it as far east as Winnipeg. By the middle of this summer we hope to have it completed to Montreal and Toronto, and we are going to press on to the maritime provinces as soon as the weather permits this spring. The situation in eastern Canada will also be developed, but it will take the remainder of this year to work things out in the maritime provinces. Until they are worked out, it is difficult to speak definitely.

What will be the main
centre in the maritime provinces?

At the present time we
are exploring the possibilities at Moncton, but no decision has been arrived at in the matter. We are considering the establishment of a terminus at Moncton with feeder services to other maritime cities.

What is the present
position of the airport on Toronto island, and what means are being provided for the rapid transport of passengers to the airport? The minister will remember that the previous government planned to build a tunnel

under the western gap, but after a lot of money had been spent the present government decided to discontinue this work. I believe a lot of the lumber that was there was shipped up to the Muncey Indian reserve, thus wasting a good deal of money.

We may have wasted a lot
of money, but I think we saved a lot at the same time in connection with that tunnel. The present plan is to use a chain ferry. I understand the distance to the mainland is only 300 yards, and it is expected that the elapsed time for a trip will not be more than five minutes.

May I come back to the
question I asked the minister with reference to Windsor? The minister may not be able to answer my question now, but when the minister said that the city of Windsor had not cooperated fully with the department I believe he had something else in mind. I should like to state that interested parties in that city are now negotiating in connection with a proposed site for an airport. The negotiations so far have been very satisfactory as far as the department is concerned, but the matter has not reached the stage where the city could be expected to commit itself one way or another. I can assure the minister that the city of Windsor and the other agencies involved are interested and are cooperating to the full.

The minister did not
answer my question with regard to the airport to take care of the Toronto situation.

Our cooperation was asked in the development of two airports, one at Malton and the other on the island. Our surveys disclosed that the Malton field had possibilities of being developed into perhaps the finest airport on the north American continent; it is almost ideal for all weather conditions. The island airport is unexcelled because of its accessibility to the business district, but it does not comply with the standard specifications in being too close to the high buildings along the water front. Our department has ascertained that for about eighty-five per cent of the time the island airport will be quite suitable, and when weather conditions do not permit its use-this is when first-class facilities are needed-the Malton field will be available.
Will the Malton airport be affected by fog?
Not so far as our observations indicate.
