speechtext: The point raised by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) is well taken. The discussion for the last few moments has been all in connection with airports, and that would come more properly under item No. 387. If we could pass this item, we could proceed to the next.
Is the department bending its energies towards taking adventure out of flying in Canada?

This particular item is solely for that purpose as it covers the regulation of flying. This vote is to ensure that aircraft are in proper condition before they leave the ground; that the rules of flying are observed, and that planes are not overloaded or are not flown in a dangerous condition.

Is some effort being made to reduce the present high landing speeds? The fact that a plane carrying pas-51952-50
sengers must land at a speed of eighty-five miles an hour may not sound dangerous, but the fact is that is a very fast speed at which to land. I am told that some of the newer machines land at speeds of 100 to 120 miles an hour. That seems still to leave adventure in flying, and I do not think you will get the people of Canada or of any other country to travel consistently by air until that factor is removed.

Very few planes have a landing speed as high as eighty-five miles per hour; the average landing speed is forty to sixty-five miles an hour. The question here is whether the runways, or, in the case of a hydroplane, whether the lake or water area is large enough to provide for landing at that speed. If the proper runway is there and fitted to the speed, there is probably no more hazard in landing at sixty-five miles an hour than at a lower speed.

Would the minister be good enough to inform the committee of the procedure followed in laying down regulations as to the airworthiness of our aircraft, the qualifications of pilots, and matters of that sort? I think it would be of great interest to know how these regulations are arrived at and1 determined.

An international convention upon airworthiness and navigation governs both those points reasonably closely. We are just now completing our new regulations as to airworthiness and requirements for pilots. They will be out very shortly, and rather than give an amateurish explanation of what is in them, I shall be very glad to send a copy of them to my hon. friend.

I was interested in asking the question because within the year we hope that large transport planes in the hands of Canadian pilots will be passing through Canadian air. We fully realize that the Canadian pilot has distinguished himself in both commercial flying and wartime flying as has no other pilot in the world, and we may justly be proud of our achievements in that field. On the other hand, we have had a limited experience with the beam method of flying in this country. It will be readily recognized that straight instrument flying and directional flying under radio control are quite different from flying by map and compass or taking one's position from the ground, and in view of that difference I understand that Trans-Canada Air Lines have brought several pilots from the United States into Canada to instruct our pilots in the art of beam flying. I am not for a moment suggesting any criticism of

Supply-Transport-Aviation

the capabilities of these gentlemen, particularly because of the extended and happy experience the United States have had in their transport and passenger flying. On the other hand, we fully realize that Imperial Airways has achieved ends which are second to none in the world; while there may be some differences between the method of flying on the European continent and other parts of the world and what we plan over here, nevertheless Imperial Airways pilots have had the experience and the training, and I would ask the minister why it is that United States pilots are being brought to Canada, rather than pilots of Imperial Airways, for the purpose of giving instruction to our own pilots.

On this continent beam flying is used. Imperial Airways uses a direction finder. They carry a spare officer, a navigator, who works out his position from the stars, and when he gets within range of homing devices he works out his position by radio direction finding. We believe that for the conditions we will encounter in the Trans-Canada service it is decidedly preferable to follow the beam type of flying. We think a plane flying at three miles a minute over mountains does not give the navigator sufficient time to plot his course as he goes along, and it would mean carrying a navigator in the plane in any event. Beam flying has been very successful in this country, and we think we are wise in choosing a proven method of transport for this continent under conditions paralleled by existing competing lines.

In addition to what the minister has just said, those of us who have flown in transport planes in both the United States and Europe, particularly on Imperial Airways and some of the German lines, or the Dutch, Swedish or Danish lines, realize that their method of flying is quite different from that which is practised in the United States. In the United States a plane sets out from an airport for another airport, and every effort is exerted to have that plane land on time. They tend to stick to the beam in spite of weather, and maintain a predetermined altitude of, say 3,500 or 4,000 feet, following the beam into the airport. Flying in Europe is done rather differently. I remember flying from Copenhagen to Stockholm a year ago. We climbed to 16,000 feet to get above bad weather; and on another occasion flying from Malmo, Sweden, to Amsterdam, Holland, we went seventy miles to the south to avoid a storm. In such flying as I have done in the United States I cannot recall instances where we have gone as far out of our way or climbed to 15,000
'Mr. Massey.]
feet except to get over a mountain. I think we all realize that Imperial Airways pilots have built up for themselves an enviable record. We all realize too that the experience of the United States airlines on some occasions, particularly on the west coast where fog is encountered, has not been too happy. Would the minister be good enough to inform the committee of the method that will be followed in Canada, whether we shall follow the example of various European lines and detour or climb in an attempt to avoid bad weather, or will our planes go straight through on the beam in spite of bad weather?

We are in a very happy position in Canada. We have our own pilots with wide experience in the type of flying that is done in Europe, where the pilot uses his own judgment to a great extent. We have, too, the facilities for beam flying, which is not at all restrictive as to the height the plane may go. The pilot can go up to ten or twelve or fifteen thousand feet if he likes, but if he leaves the beam he loses all benefit from it and must rely on homing devices. He has the further advantage, if he can stay on the beam, of getting his definite location and of having instructions over the beam to duplicate his radio direction finding instructions. So we believe he is in a better and safer position than the pilot in the Imperial Airways plane. Of course, the Imperial Airways plane travels under quite different circumstances. It would be almost impossible to have the beam on many of the routes they fly. The planes leave England and go out over the ocean, and the carrying power of the beam is not very great. The maximum distance for which the beam can be relied upon is two hundred miles. I think we are very well safeguarded. Our pilots have been examined by several experienced aviators, and I have been told on all sides that we have to-day twenty-one pilots who are the equal of any that can be produced in any country in the world. They are well trained in our type of bush flying; that is, flying without aids to navigation, and we have taken the best of them and have given them a thorough training in beam flying with capable instructors brought here for the purpose.

Our pilots are indeed,
the best in the world. It is generally understood that within the next few months, or perhaps a year or two, Imperial Airways will have a round-the-world service. There are few places now where they have not a service, one of the few gaps left to complete, to make that service an actuality, being across

Canada, and another over the Atlantic ocean where experiments were so successfully conducted last summer. For this round-the-world service of Imperial Airways, will Canadian pilots fly Canadian planes across Canada, or will the British pilots take the Imperial Airways planes from Australia, or whatever point they take off from, and use our facilities here, flying their own ships across our dominion?
Canadian planes and Canadian pilots will always do the flying over Canada.

Will the minister give
the committee some information regarding the service to the Yukon? A considerable volume of support came forward to the work which the Vancouver board of trade did in endeavouring to persuade the minister that the route which would serve the Yukon most successfully was from Vancouver. Their plea largely was that for thirty years the principal service of supplies to the Yukon had been carried on via Vancouver, and they were naturally anxious to keep that connection. I believe the minister was of opinion that, at the present time at least, it would not be possible to carry on that service via Vancouver. Will the minister state how far have negotiations to that end been carried on. and whether he considers that the time will shortly come when the arrangements for commercial flying Vancouver to Ashcroft to Prince George will be made use of as a feeder to the Canada Air Lines?

At the moment, Edmonton
is linked with the Yukon by a private service, with a mail contract from the post office. Test flights are being made for a route from Vancouver to Ashcroft to Prince George, and also, I understand, by the Pacific coast, but to date I believe no mail contracts have been awarded. The matter of lines of this sort is really outside our jurisdiction as far as initiating them goes. The lines must show that they have sufficient traffic to develop an air mail contract substantial enough to justify the service.

Has	the Department of
Transport anything whatever to say as to the routes that are to be opened up across different parts of Canada? Surely some department of the government should be able to give a lead in these matters or should have some control over what routes are flown. Can a man set up an air route and carry passengers anywhere he wishes in Canada without any check by the government as to what route he is to fly?

Our act prescribes the conditions under which he must fly. If necessity is shown for a route; if the post office department-can be interested or even if they cannot if a route is to be flown, our inspectors pass on the equipment and on the landing facilities, they investigate whether the lakes are sufficiently large to permit planes to land in safety, and the whole route is inspected before it is licensed. We are adopting now a licensing system. If a plane is flying a route with any regularity-once a day or a week or a month-the route is licensed to that party after our inspectors have determined that conditions along the route make for safety of operation.

The reason I raise the question is that the development of the Yukon air mail route has been most unfair. It may be that the government did not intend to be unfair in acting as they have done; but they have given this air mail subsidy to a line flying from Edmonton to the Yukon, whereas practically all the passenger, the express and the freight business to the Yukon has come for many years from Vancouver and other coast points. The result of subsidizing this air mail service from Edmonton to the Yukon will be to deprive the coast cities of that business, and the government should have power to prevent or stop that sort of thing; it should not have been allowed in the first place. Flying is going on from Vancouver to the Yukon, I believe that route can be flown in a shorter time than the other, and surely that is the way by which this service should operate. I would ask the minister to have the matter looked into and see if these conditions cannot be righted, because the effect is to take business away from the coast cities and give it to Edmonton, and that in my opinion is not at all fair.

The hon. member who has just taken his seat apparently overlooks the fact that there are a great many intermediate points between Edmonton and the destination to be served. I feel sure that the present move is the right one, simply because it provides the only means of communication available to the people of the interior. So far as the time required is concerned, I doubt if that has a great deal to do with the matter, because after all the object of the service should be to do as much good as possible, and in that connection time is a secondary factor. In my opinion the post office, in doing what they did, have done a very good job.

Surely
the hon. member for Vancouver South
Supply-Transport-Aviation

spoke without a knowledge of the actual conditions in connection with proper communication by air from all parts of Canada and from the United States, and prospectively, the round-the-world mail service which will be inaugurated. The very arguments that he gave are, I should say, in favour of the route as established. The route from Edmonton to the Yukon has been opened up by private capital to satisfy an imperative demand not only for passenger but for mail service. I doubt whether this is the proper time to develop the argument, but surely the route has been selected after careful inspection and investigation by technical advisers of the Department of Transport. Surely no route should be used except and until it has been fully investigated by the proper technical officials.

It is a misnomer to speak of a mail "subsidy." The carriage of mails is remunerated not as a subsidy but as a payment for a service, and I understand that the post office has found that on the whole it is a profitable enterprise. The reason the route was flown north from Edmonton was, of course, that it was demonstrated that sufficient mail offered to justify the service, which is weekly. It has proved profitable to the post office I am sure that if it can be demonstrated that any other route is similarly profitable to the post office, there will not be any difficulty about arranging a payment for the service.

Why should this matter be left to the post office? Should not the Department of Transport decide what routes shall 'be flown? The hon. member for Edmonton West led the committee to believe that the department inspected the route from Edmonton to the Yukon. If they did that, they should at the same time have inspected the route from Vancouver to the Yukon. I do not know whether they inspected either route. Perhaps they just did not pay attention to anything that was happening, with the result that the Pacific coast has been put in a very unfavourable position. As to mail coming from the United States, that is just what we are afraid of, that the larger American centres in the east have been favouring this route from Edmonton to the Yukon and that this service has been inaugurated for their benefit, which we think is not fair to the Pacific coast
As regards the service to the orient, Australia and New Zealand, we have alw'ays been led to believe that it would go direct from Vancouver, but now we hear about this route via Alaska. It seems to me these are matters in which the Department of Transport should take some interest; it should not be just a

dog fight to see who gets in first. Plans should be carefully thought out ahead, and the best route for all parties concerned selected.

We
who have lived in western Canada for some considerable time know that, in the past, attempts have been made to make water run up-hill. I do not think the Department of Transport should for a moment allow petty jealousies, one city or one part of a province against another, to enter into the matter at all. In my opinion the traffic should find the easiest route and should be encouraged along that line.

By the same token, I
have no doubt that the minister will be glad to hear of that route which is closest, safest and most advantageous from the standpoint of aerial development. Much has been said by hon. members who have spoken previously in regard to aerial connection with the great republic to the south, and I am informed that the most direct route from the south, from the western states of the south, is by way of San Francisco or Los Angeles over the Rocky mountains, crossing the great American desert to Glendive, North Dakota; from there to the queen city of the west, Regina; from Regina north to Saskatoon and Prince Albert; from Prince Albert north to Goldfields; from there up to Yellow Knife; thence to Aklavik, and on to the Yukon.
That is the safest and shortest route, and it avoids the perils of the Pacific ocean and the hazards of the Rocky mountains. Airmen themselves would very much prefer to have that chosen as the route leading into the great north, and there is another reason why that route should be very carefully considered, It may not be generally known to hon. members, but in the province of Saskatchewan in the great hinterland there are about 80.000 square miles of the pre-Cambrian shield. The pre-Cambrian shield houses all the resources that are responsible for the mineral wealth of Ontario and Quebec, and in Saskatchewan there are 80,000 square miles of it. It has been developed on the east at Flinflon and on the west at Goldfields, and between these two points there is a great natural wealth that would arouse the envy of the Incas of Peru. We know that wealth is there and we are seeking the cooperation of all the departments of government and in particular the Department of Transport in the development of that territory. It is Saskatchewan's one hope for a well balanced and better economy.

I should like to get a word of support from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie).

Supply-Transport-Aviation
Speak to him.

I will speak to him all right. Seriously, I believe there is now a regular air service in operation between Vancouver and the Yukon, and I understood from what the minister said that his department could examine routes and license them if they were satisfactory. Is there any reason why that route should not be examined in the near future and a licence issued if the route were found satisfactory? We would then be in a position to have the air mail which is going from Vancouver to the Yukon flown up the coast or through the interior up to Prince George and from there to the Yukon. We do object, and rightly so, to having the business taken from under our nose.

Apparently we were out of order in discussing airports and we are out of order now in discussing airways. I wish to say something about this matter; but I hesitate to be out of order because the hon. member for Halifax is in his place, and I am afraid that we might have a speech to-night on the Crimean war if any irrelevant discussion were allowed. Am I in order in discussing airways?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When the committee passes item No. 386, the hon. gentleman will be in order.
May I ask the minister for an answer to my question?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: That comes properly under item No. 387. Shall item No. 386 carry?

This item is for the control of civil aviation, and it is in regard to that subject that we wish to ask a few questions. The other evening the minister did me the high honour of indicating to a gathering in the city of Ottawa that it was probable that I would oppose a certain proposal which he was going to make to the House of Commons. It is not usual to discuss these matters at banquets before they are heard of in the house, but to other days and other manners these things were different. First of all, I would ask this question:	Under this item are
the gentlemen to whom the minister alluded on that festive occasion being paid?
No; this is purely the administration of the department's control of civil aviation.
It has nothing at all to do with the operations of the plants?
No.

That settles that question for the moment; it will come up under the next item. Might I ask my second question, which arises out of what has been said. It is this: To whom did the department award the contract for the carriage of mails from Edmonton to the Yukon?
That is a matter for the Post Office Department, but I happen to know that it is Grant McConnachie of United Airways.
Does the minister know how he came into possession of the contract?
No.
The Post Office Department will enlighten us on that?
Quite so.

Then this item does not bear in any way upon the matters to which the minister alluded the other evening, or yet upon the circumstances under which this young man became possessed of this contract, having come without one and left here with it? There is nothing here that will assist us in dealing with that question. This is departmental control?
Yes.
Thank you. We will discuss the matter when we come to it.

The
leader of the opposition made a slighting remark in reference to a young man of the city I have the honour to represent in this house. The young man is Grant McConnachie, and he is merely an official of a substantial, reliable, aggressive company which has made a contract with the Post Office Department.

I am not making any slighting observations with reference to him. On the contrary I would compliment him upon his ability to secure a contract by an act almost of legerdemain in pulling the rabbit out. He pulled, and out it came. That is what I had reference to. Do not worry about any slighting observations about one who is thus able to pull the trick he pulled under the circumstances under which it was done. You put your hand in, shut your eyes and pull out a mail contract to carry mails from Vancouver to the Yukon with the high approval of the order in council for which the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) must be partly responsible. That is not a matter of importance at the moment. The minister does not know anything about it?

No.
Supply-Transport-Airways

I thought not. That would be nothing unusual. I think you are entitled to that. So the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. MacKinnon) is entirely wrong in suggesting that I am in any sense indicating that any slighting observations should be made about one who is able to do this legerdemain trick, about which we shall receive particulars when we come to the Post Office Department, and the wonders that such a distinguished and shall I say courageous and active young man can accomplish. So I leave it at that. The Post Office Department is to enlighten our ignorance, I understand, and if the Minister of National Defence is to help us with his knowledge it will be received with great pleasure and satisfaction when that vote is reached.

Item agreed to.
Airways and airports-construction and improvements including lighting and radio facilities (capital), $1,722,400.
May I get an answer to my question?

Wihat was the question?
I did not hear a question.
The question was whether or not it would be possible for the department to check this new route that is being flown from Vancouver to the Yukon, and license it if it is found to be in order.

There is no direct route from Vancouver to the Y'ukon up the coast. It is too foggy for safe flying at the moment. There is a route being developed from Vancouver to Ashcroft and Fort George and Fort St. John, whore it ties in with the operation from Edmonton to the Yukon. I understand there is also a route being developed direct from Vancouver to Prince George via Hazelton. As I say, the speed with which these routes are developed will depend entirely on the amount of traffic. These are private enterprises and private canital is very anxious to explore every possibility of making a profit. If it can be demonstrated1 that either of these routes has the necessary traffic, I am sure that the Post Office Department will make the necessary arrangements to carry the mail and the route will be developed. If it is reported that anyone desires to fly the route, our inspectors will go in and if the route complies with the requirements we will license it. We are not retarding development but on the other hand the establishment of a route will depend on the traffic that offers. Traffic is the criterion.
The department is in a position to check a route at any time?
Quite.
Can the minister tell us what improvements are being made under this vote in the airports in western Canada?
Does my hon. friend want a detailed report on each one?
I think it would be well to put on Hansard a short statement regarding each one.

Will the minister permit me to interrupt? I think it would be of great assistance to the committee and to all concerned if he would give a general picture as to the position of Trans-Canada Air Lines with an estimate as to when we may expect the inauguration of passenger and freight service.

Starting from the western end we have at Vancouver one of the finest airports on the continent. It is well located and well developed, has concrete runways and is in first-class condition. Then we have an auxiliary airport at Langley Prairie. The grading of three landing strips is completed, and seeding is taking place there. I think by midsummer Langley will be in condition for use; it is an emergency landing field. Then at Hope the field is usable; there is a little more work to be done this summer; this is also an emergency landing field. At Princeton the field is usable, and there is very little to be done there; the radio beam is in, power installed. The radio beam is in at Vancouver as well. Then at Oliver the lighting is finished and the runways serviced; that landing field is complete. At Midway the field is usable, that is only an emergency field. At Grand Forks the radio range is in and consideration is being given there to an alternative field, as the municipal field is not capable of being developed up to standard. At Trail there is a municipal airport sufficient for emergency landings. At Salmo the field is completed, but the lighting is not installed. At Cranbrook municipal airport the lighting is now being installed, and the department is installing two-way radio equipment. At Lethbridge the old municipal airport was found to be unsuitable and a new airport has been selected; lighting is installed; the beam is ready and the field is now in fair condition for use. Trans-Canada Air Lines is building a hangar there. The next principal field is Medicine Hat; there again the field is usable; the lighting equipment is ready for

Supply-Transport-Airways
service; the power line for the radio range is completed and I believe the radio range is on the air now. Then Swift Current-
What about Calgary?
We have a difficult problem there. The old field is not capable of being developed to modem standards, but at the same time it is usable in ordinary weather.
You have a lighthouse there, and power?

Yes, but if the weather is too unfavourable we cannot stop at Calgary; we will have to fly on to Edmonton. We are hoping, possibly this season, to work out a new field there. I have tried to induce my colleague the Minister of National Defence to let us use his very fine field, but so far without success.
We will remember that!

Perhaps from there on a general statement would do. The Trans-Canada airways from Winnipeg west is to all intents and purposes completed, and regular flights will take place from about March 1. For a time, while the flights will be on regular schedule, only mail will be carried; but after the weather improves and we are sure that all arrangements are working well we will take passengers as far east as Winnipeg.
Coming east from Winnipeg on the ordinary route, flying will be done at night, and we are putting in lighting fixtures and complete radio beams. The fields are all well developed right through to Toronto.
At what points?

Winnipeg, Kenora, Sioux
Lookout, Wagaming, Nakina, Pagwa, Kapus-kasing, Porquis Junction, North Bay, Reay and Toronto, and then Ottawa and Montreal. We expect that that route will be in the same position as the western end by the first of July. We expect to be able to run planes from Montreal to Winnipeg and Vancouver on July 1.
You do not fly over the lakes?
No; the route is around the north.

What
points will the route touch between Toronto and Ottawa?

I do not know whether the hon. member knows the names of the places I have mentioned. Some of them are very small places. The route, however, is Montreal, Ottawa, Killaloe, Bracebridge, Reay and Toronto.

When will there be a regular schedule from the Atlantic to -the Pacific coast, and when will the operation take place? Would it run once a week, once a month, or how often? When can we expect a regular trans-Canada air line service to be operating on regular schedule?

If the hon. member will accept the St. Lawrence river as the Atlantic, then I would say that we can expect a regular daily schedule beginning July 1 of this year, operating between Montreal and Vancouver.
But we do not accept that.
It is expected that planes will leave Montreal about eight in the evening and arrive in Vancouver at noon the next day.

We in the maritime provinces have too long accepted the St. Lawrence river as the eastern terminus of Canada. If this were a railway I could understand why we might have to start at one point and complete the work, section by section; but as it is to be an airway service, I do not see why ports in the east could not be developed at the same time as ports in central or western Canada. We in the maritime provinces have been on the tail end of many things for a long time, and I should like to see something done to give us the service we deserve. The suggestion that the St. Lawrence river might be considered the Atlantic ocean is a little too far-fetched for us from that end of Canada to swallow.

The hon. member will see
a great deal of activity in the maritimes this year. Our main expenditures in the coming year will be in the development of the service in the maritime provinces. The difficulty, of course, is that we can ask parliament only for limited funds to apply on the work in any one year. We hope that the end of this year we may have a trans-Canada service from coast to coast, and that by this time next year the planes will be flying the entire distance.

The route the minister set out was from Montreal to Ottawa and, as I followed him, to North Bay. I was wondering if he had anticipated going from Ottawa to Toronto and then to North Bay. What is the direct route we may expect? If Toronto is on a branch line, I should like to hear what the minister has to say about it.

The first planes will fly over the route, as I suggested, from Montreal to Ottawa, to Reay and to Toronto and then
Supply-Transport-Airways

back to Reay and on to North Bay, and west. As traffic develops, it is quite probable that we shall be able to run separate planes from Montreal and from Toronto.
The same as the trains?
Yes.

I would like the minister to tell us how we are to get to and from the island at Toronto. We have been listening to information about the fine ports at Regina, Vancouver, Edmonton and elsewhere, and realizing that the taxes collected in Toronto are a large per cent of those collected throughout Canada, I think it is about time that Toronto had some of those fine ports.
The minister said something about a chain ferry. I must confess I do not know anything about that.

Maybe it is like a
chain letter.

I do not know about
chain ferries running across the bay, but would the minister tell us about the chain ferry?
You pull yourself over.

The minister said it would be a lot faster than that. When the tunnel was first planned by the late government, it was stated that passengers could go from the Royal York, the King Edward or any other downtown points in Toronto to the air port within five or ten minutes. But I can picture them taking about an hour by a chain ferry, particularly if it is stormy weather. The minister will have to give the Queen city of all Canada a much better entry to the island than would be afforded by a chain ferry.

While there have been
several things said-
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The hon.
member for Halifax has the floor.

I thank you, Mr. Chairman,
that I have the floor. I am able to stand on both feet. "There is no wooden leg about this," as in the pensions debate.
I have followed very closely the remarks of the Minister of Transport in connection with the development of the airways. So far as the route from Montreal to the east is concerned, it seems to me everything is in the air, but there is nothing up there to travel in. I was very much surprised when he said that the second emergency station would be

"Hope." I remember once coming up from Bermuda in the old "Alpha", and while in a fog getting off our course. We got in touch with a little schooner to find out where we were, and learned that we were off Little Hope light. The name of the schooner was "Our Only Joy." So I guess the schooner is our only joy, so far as the aeroplane service is concerned.
What was in the schooner?

You will have to ask the "Admiral." Then we come to another stop which bears a great name; it sounds something like "Grand Fox." One has to be pretty foxy to follow some of these things. Then we come down to Swift Current; things are so swift that, so far as the east is concerned, we are swept off our feet.
In all sincerity I must say that I have no desire to be too critical, but it does seem to me that in the east we have been forgotten. If we did not remember that we existed and did not sometimes get to our feet-as seldom we do-we would not be known at all.
Halifax is the eastern gateway of Canada as Vancouver is the western, but there is no intimation by the minister that he hopes at some future time to extend this service eastwards. Is the eastern terminus of this air line to be in the adjoining province of New Brunswick? What will be the route from Montreal east, and where will be the point of departure on the Atlantic? I am not referring to the St. Lawrence as that is an inland waterway. Millions have been spent on that in order to permit ships with slightly greater draught than the Empress of Britain to follow that waterway to Montreal. WTould the minister give us an outline of what is proposed in airways east of Montreal? Can he tell us what is to be done for the maritimes and for that part of Quebec east of Montreal? I should like to know where the ships are to take off for overseas and the Mediterranean.

The line runs from Montreal to within a few miles of Sherbrooke, across the state of Maine to about half way between St. John and Fredericton, and then to Moncton. The intention is to operate non-stop from Montreal to Moncton. This route has been chosen in an effort to avoid fog, the great enemy of flying. Almost anything else can be overcome except fog. We believe we have a route almost entirely free of that menace. From Moncton east it is intended to ask private enterprise to join with us in setting up routes. There is already a private route from Moncton to Charlottetown-and we hope to have routes to Halifax, Saint John and Sydney.

Supply-Transport-Airways

I do not think the statement of the minister is quite satisfactory. We have one illustration of transportation going through the state of Maine. On the Canadian Pacific railway it is a case of closed doors after you leave Megantic until you cross the state. It is now proposed to run this air line across the state of Maine instead of through Canadian territory. We are a long way from Montreal, and there is no indication that any service is to be given beyond Moncton, except that provided by private companies. We are not to be part of a trans-Canada scheme of air lines to be paid for by the people of this country for the good of the people in the east as well as in the west. As one of the representatives for Halifax I am not satisfied with this proposed service. We have just as much right to the security of the best planes as have the people between Vancouver and Montreal and Saint John and Moncton. There is a dead stop when you get to Moncton; from then on you take your choice between "give me liberty or give me death" by private planes.

In the discussion
concerning this air line no mention seems to be made of connections with the United States lines. Surely some consideration has been given to linking up with the United States lines south of the Niagara peninsula. Could the minister give us some idea of what connections are contemplated?

There are two obvious
connections. One is from Toronto to Buffalo, to connect with the United States lines to New York and the east. The other is from Toronto to Windsor, to connect with the lines to Detroit, Chicago and the west. We have had preliminary discussions; but nothing definite has been developed, although we expect that a decision will be reached shortly. My hon. friend knows that at the present time there are connections between Montreal and New York, between Winnipeg and Minneapolis and St. Paul, and between Vancouver and Seattle.

I did not have the
advantage of hearing the earlier discussion on this matter, but in answering the last question the minister referred to Windsor. I should like to know the situation with respect to that city. I realize that Windsor is not on the main line of the trans-Canada airways, but I should like to know just what the minister has in mind in connection with that city.

I gave that information
earlier in the discussion. We have been in
constant touch with Windsor, and at the present time the obvious site is being used in a small way.

When matters of this kind are up for discussion, we hear much about Toronto, Vancouver, Windsor and Halifax-perhaps I should have put Halifax first-but there are many people who consider Hamilton to be of more importance. Could the minister tell me how Hamilton will be tied up with the route from Toronto to Chicago and the trans-Canada route?
Hamilton is in the centre of traffic on the route west. Planes will pass there each day, and I am sure they will stop if traffic offers.
Is the present route between Toronto and Ottawa the most direct? I have in mind that the railway systems follow a more southern course. What were the determining factors in deciding on this route?

In deciding a route for this type of transportation the density of population is not important as planes do not stop very often. In this case the only stops will be at Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto; anything in between will be handled by another service. On this route the minimum of new fields are required. When planes travel at the rate of three miles per minute, the fact that they must go a few miles further is not very serious in the matter of time.

It has been interesting for the members from the maritimes to listen to the Minister of Transport outline the various actions taken to provide services for the western portion of Canada. On looking at the report I find that there are already six districts in operation, each with a superintendent. There is one at each of these cities: Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa. From the report and the statement made by the Minister of Transport, it seems that the service is to stop at the St. Lawrence. I am in hearty accord with the view expressed by my colleague from Halifax (Mr. Finn), and I would impress upon the minister that we in the east feel that we are entitled to the same consideration as those in the extreme west. We are not envious of western members, but we ask for similar treatment for the east, and I think that is only a fair request to make. We do not think it is fair to have only one station for the whole three maritime provinces on the Trans-Canada Air Lines, and from there to have to depend
Supply-Transport-Airways

on commercial lines. I understand the commercial companies have on more than one occasion applied for a licence in the maritimes to give us an air service while we are waiting for the Trans-Canada service to be inaugurated, and that the licence has always been refused. I should like to know from the minister whether he has in the past received applications for a licence in the maritime provinces and whether they have been refused; whether he has similar applications before him at the present time, and what likelihood there is of a licence being granted so that we may get a service at once pending the extension of the Trans-Canada Air Lines service. I should also like to ask when the service from Halifax to Vancouver will be in operation.

The situation in the maritimes has received most careful study from those competent to decide how that section of the country can best be served. We have a route from Montreal to Moncton which can be flown, as far as we can see, pretty close to 365 days in the year; but when we fly from Moncton to the coast in any direction we have fog, and the service is likely to be interrupted. It was thought, therefore, that in the interests of the service the route from Montreal to Moncton should be established, so that deliveries could be made at least to Moncton every day in the year. We have one of the oldest services in Canada flying between Moncton and Charlottetown. It is licensed by our department and has been operating for a good many years with a good deal of success. I think I am safe in saying before another sixteen months is past, I can guarantee my friends from the maritimes that we shall have an entirely adequate service connecting Moncton with the principal cities of the maritime provinces, and with equipment entirely adequate for that service.
In reply to my hon. friend's other question, we have had applications for a licence for the maritime provinces; but we have refused to grant them for the very reason I gave on the previous vote, that before granting a licence we required the ground facilities to be adequate. The ground facilities in the maritimes were not adequate, and therefore we refused to grant the licences. But the planes insisted on flying, and of a fleet of five planes I think two are still intact. Fortunately there was no great loss of life. Until we get these facilities, which we shall endeavour to complete this year, we are not going to grant licences to fly in the maritime provinces.
I do not think the minister was quite fair to the maritimes in his statement. He talks about accidents and death. Did they take place in the air or at the landing fields?
Landing fields.

Not at the landing field in Halifax. The sum of S65,000 has to be spent in connection with the air field there, and nothing has been done. I think we are entitled to something a little more definite than the minister's statement that we shall have a service within sixteen months or two years.

The minister, in replying to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) in reference to transportation from Toronto island to the mainland said that he would put on a chain ferry. Now a chain ferry, as I have known them, is a kind of scow with a chain fastened on both sides of the opening and drawn through the scow, bringing the scow across from one side to the other. It is a very slow means of transportation, and certainly it would not fit in with the wonderful service the minister is anticipating giving to the people of Canada. I know Toronto bay very well, having had boats on the bay for a number of years, and I understand there is a great number of speed boats in Toronto bay which would be available and could transport airplane passengers from the island to the city very much better than any chain ferry. I think it would be possible for the minister to have these speed boats transport passengers from the point where the airplanes will land to the foot of York street, which is within four hundred yards of the union station, within a little more than five minutes, and I do not think the cost would be very great. I would suggest, therefore, that the minister give consideration, as a temporary means of transportation at all events, to using speed boats for transporting airplane passengers from the island to the city.

So far as the service between the island and the city is concerned, that is entirely a matter for the city of Toronto. The airports are both owned by the city of Toronto. We contribute part of the cost. Toronto will operate the airports, and we [DOT]will lease from that city certain facilities which we require.

Then so far as the government is concerned, the island being the airport, that will be the place to dump off passengers for Toronto! Just dump them off at the island! Never mind about how they

Supply-Transport-Airways
get to Toronto! Dump them off at the island -as if that was their destination! Is that what the minister means?

We shall certainly demand
that transportation be provided from the island or we shall not go there.

I have two things to commend the minister for, first for his efficient staff, a representative of which visited the head of the lakes this summer. I was appalled at the amount of work that had to be done before a landing field could be brought into existence. It is necessary for cities themselves to be air-minded, as this committee seems to be to-night, and it is necessary for the city to cooperate in providing landing facilities. We shall have at the head of the lakes a landing field that will not be surpassed even by the one at Vancouver, and anybody from the east who wants to visit the great wheat fields of Saskatchewan will find a nice cool spot at the head of the lakes to land, because Fort William passed their by-law yesterday.
Another thing for which I would commend the minister is that not even a cabinet minister will get a free ride in these planes. That means that there will not be any passes even for members of parliament. We should commend the minister for this unselfish act.

I was quite disappointed when I heard the minister outline the air service as regards the maritime provinces. It is almost enough to make persons coming from the maritime provinces feel that they were ostracized as far as airport services were concerned.

You ostracize yourself by
living there.

We feel that we are
still a part of Canada; we have supported every move for the benefit of Canada; our people are spread over every part of the dominion; our ancestors were pioneers in most of the services that originated since Canada was Canada. It comes down to this, that the maritime provinces have been left out in the cold to a very great extent, since the Canadian National railways took over the Intercolonial railway. I do not blame the minister at all for this; but it is just one more instance of the fact that our civil service appointees, men who have probably been long in the service, and "know it all," cast their eyes over Canada and say, "This is for this, and that is for that." Is there any person who has the least inkling of what is going on in Canada to-day who will contend that
the dominion can, on the one hand, get rid of government responsibility in the transportation of passengers from Moncton to Halifax and Sydney and, on the other, assume full responsibility for transportation, machines and equipment, airport facilities and everything else from Moncton west? [DOT]
As regards the provision of facilities from Moncton east we know that even under today's conditions fog is practically no impediment, because the beam ray will take planes in. We know that it took planes in from the Pacific coast in the height of fog, because, listening over the radio, we were told of the arrival of Miss Earhart's plane when she landed in San Francisco, and there was a severe fog at the time. That, in spite of all the improvements which have been made, all the equipment which has been provided, and the vast amount of money which the dominion is asked to vote for air services, one of the oldest provinces of Canada is to be left without proper facilities, redounds to the discredit of the aviation branch of the dominion government.

I do not know much about
air services; but I observe that the government is about to spend approximately one and three-quarter million dollars, and I see that the minister is being pestered on all sides by hon. members from every part of the country suggesting that their particular locality is the best place to spend this money on. My suggestion to the minister is to take very little notice of appeals of this kind. He should be guided solely by what he considers is the best advice obtainable from the most competent officials. That being done, I do not care what part of the country gets the service. Sometimes we regard Canada as the centre of the universe, and Winnipeg may be the centre of Canada, but I am not asking particularly for any service in Winnipeg if the requirements are not there to justify it. I do say this, that one hon. member after another in this chamber should not rise in his place and demand from the minister certain facilities if the services are not required. If they are required in the mari-times, I am satisfied to leave it to the minister and his officials to provide the necessary facilities.
You do not represent the mari-times.

I may say with reference to the maritimes that $300,000 have been spent. We have fields under way at Upper Brockway, Blissville, Cambridge, Havelock, Moncton, West Brook and Stanley, and we have

Supply- Transport-A irwa ys
fairly adequate municipal fields at Moncton, Saint John, Halifax, New Glasgow and Sydney. We have good municipal fields at Charlottetown and Summerside. With the work we expect to do there this year we believe that the maritime provinces will be as well equipped as any other part of Canada.

In view of the statement the minister has made as to the amount of money already spent, can he give the committee some idea as to what the revenues are likely to be after all the fields have been equipped and the services are in operation?
The hon. member means, the revenue for the use of the fields?
All told.

It is very hard to estimate that. There is no service now. We are starting from zero to build a service. We anticipate that it will be self-supporting from the start. Just how long it will take to make the fields themselves self-supporting I cannot say.

Having listened to those who are getting the cream of the service, and not wishing to speak for my own constituency in particular, I believe quite a number of members will be interested in knowing whether there is any general policy with reference to feeder lines, if at a later date the minister can say what policy will be adopted in so far as the Canadian airways are concerned as to feeders into the main trans-Canada system. Many cities and areas of considerable settlement are off the main air line, and I believe that a large part of the country would be interested in knowing if there is any policy or any anticipated policy as to how that situation will be dealt with.

As I said before, it altogether depends on the traffic that will originate on a route of that kind. If there is a real advantage in moving mail by aeroplane rather than by train, there will probably be a reason for the route and revenues to warrant its establishment. It all depends on that. Anywhere that private enterprise can find a profitable operation, they will undoubtedly apply to the post office for payment for a mail service, which is the back-bone of all operations.
That will be by private enterprise?
Private enterprise.

May I remind the hon. member for Winnipeg North, dealing with the statement that we from the maritimes should leave all these matters of policy to the minister, that we are quite willing to do that if the west will follow the same policy.
[Mr. Howe.J
So far as I am concerned, I am quite willing.

As I understood from the minister, the policy of the department is to have a centre station at Moncton and then connect with other cities. Did the minister mean only cities in the maritimes, or towns, or districts? Are we to take it literally that the orders are to connect only with the cities?
I should perhaps have said, large centres of traffic.

I also am rather in disagreement with some of the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North. In referring a few minutes ago to Hamilton, I am sure the minister knows I did not ask him to spend one cent there. I would, however, ask him what his findings were when he visited that city last summer, as to whether the city is cooperating, and just what the conditions were as he found them.
The situation at Hamilton was very fully explored. A tentative agreement was drawn up by our department, and we are waiting for the city of Hamilton to execute it Then we shall be ready to proceed.

I was not in the chamber when the discussion started this evening on the main transcontinental air line. From the standpoint of the province of Saskatchewan and the constituency of North Battleford there are some aspects of this transportation problem by air that are interesting and important. I wish to stress a few of these. For instance, there is the trans-Canada air line passing through the southern part of the province from Winnipeg to Lethbridge. I understand that the main port of call, in fact the only one, is Regina, and that will develop air business east and west; but it does not touch the northern nor the central part of the province at all.
The whole trend of business and population now is northward and this will continue, not only during the next ten years but decades after that. Consequently, from the standpoint of air development there are other angles of the question that are of great importance. Take, for instance, trade into the north. I understand that the minister is dealing largely with the main air line and the development of business on that line and, therefore, I shall not go into the question of northern development by air to-night. I shall do that again. It is, however, becoming more important every year, and places from which that northern air business will be developed- and is developing-will be the leading points across the northern part of the province, North Battleford, Prince Albert, Melfort and so on.

Next, there is the feeder air line service. I understand that this service into Regina will be a five city tie-up which will include Regina, Moose Jaw, North Battleford, Saskatoon and Prince Albert. If the minister has not made a complete statement with reference to this feeder air service, I should like to have a few words from him in that regard if he has anything important to mention.

I understand that the Post Office Department is now calling for tenders for the service to serve these cities. The schedule has been prepared by that department to suit their requirements, and it is expected that the contract will be awarded shortly.

I appreciate the fact that money is necessary for the development of trans-Canada airways, and for Canada what is contemplated is a large expenditure. Can the minister tell us whether the department has made any estimates of the approximate deficits which will be incurred in connection with airways for the next five or six years?

The airways divide themselves into two parts, one being simply operation, the other the maintenance of airports. Trans-Canada Air Lines will handle the operation and it is thought that this will be selfsupporting from the start; but as regards revenue from the air fields, it is hopeless to expect any return until there is a greater density of traffic than exists at the initial stage. One plane landing per day at a field will not pay the operating expenses of that field. It is difficult to say how many years it will be before the fields themselves pay their operating expenses.
The minister says it is hard to tell us how long it will be before they pay their way. We should like to know what the cost will be. Is it going to be $5, or $500, or $50,000,000 or what?

The cost of operating the department's fields-radio and weather service- is a little short of a million dollars a year. We shall recover a little of that but, in the initial stages, very little. There will be some revenue from the use of the fields.

Can the minister tell us approximately when the five city daily air feeder service from Regina, through Moose Jaw, Saskatoon, North Battleford, to Prince Albert and back to Regina will likely commence?
That matter is not within the jurisdiction of this department, but I assume, from the developments which are taking place, that it will be around June or July.

The hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) has taken us back to Saskatchewan, and I would ask one or two questions relative to that province. Can the minister give us some details with regard to the airport now in course of construction south of the town of Broadview, Saskatchewan, and why the landing field that had been established near the town of Broadview was abandoned? That was a port on which there had been a considerable expenditure for improvements and it was a nice level field taking in nearly a quarter section. I should like to know why it was abandoned and a field some eight or ten miles further south taken instead. At the same time, would the minister give us some details with respect to the amount that will be expended on improving the airport at Regina. I have asked all these questions at once because it is difficult to get the floor.

The Broadview airport was leased by the government. The field was about fifteen miles off the straight line; we straightened the line and put the beams on, and we found it desirable to purchase another piece of property at Broadview. The land cost $1,486.50.
How many acres?

Roughly, a square mile.
Answering the question with regard to Regina, the department contributed $48,000 to the Regina field this year, which is the amount the city is entitled to, having regard to the amount the city itself spent. The Broadview field is 585^ acres.
In a return tabled it was given as thirty acres.

That thirty acres is the site for the beacon, the radio beam station. That is away from the main airport; I was referring to the main airport at Broadview. Two miles away from that, thirty acres of land were taken over for the radio beam, but that is another transaction.

Reading this item, I notice in brackets after it the word "capital." I take it that this is a capital expenditure and I shall be glad if the minister will explain it; that is, the capital set-up, how much has been invested in this way, and whether in that is included the cost of fields which were established some years ago under a relief program. What is the capital investment, how is it set up and how is this to be paid? Is it to be paid by borrowing? In the public works department, where we had a capital expenditure it was not paid out of revenue at all. The expenditure on the airway

to date is about $9,000,000, including the money spent under relief votes. About $5,000,000 has been expended by the civil aviation branch directly. This, I understand, has all been charged to revenue.

In view of the fact that federal engineers have been running lines on Kootenay flats in the vicinity of Creston, is the minister in a position to say whether the construction of a landing field at that point is being considered?

A field is being considered there. It is a wide valley; we would like to have a field that is capable of being approached as a blind landing, but we have not finally decided yet to establish a field at Creston.

In view of the fact that the industry at Trail is credited with having the largest export mail of any industry in the dominion, is the minister in a position to suggest what means of reaching the main lines of service will be followed?
iMr. HOWE: I am not able to do that at the moment. The matter of stops and subsidiary services is largely one for the Post Office Department to work out. We operate this service largely to meet the requirements of the Post Office Department. As far as our own operation goes, of course the fewer stops we have the better it suits us.

What arrangements are
being made or what are the plans in connection with taking mail from incoming ships either at Halifax or in the gulf of St. Lawrence? At present there is, I believe, a service that runs from Montreal and Quebec to Rimouski-or is it Father Point-and mail is taken from the transatlantic ships there and flown to those ports. Is it the intention to continue that service and also to extend the service to and from Halifax in the winter?

We have a service in summer from Father Point to Montreal. That service will be continued this year, and when the transatlantic service starts both services will be combined. Naturally we shall move all the mail we can by air.
That would apply only to the Bummer months?
Yes.
What about the winter?
What is the position as to the radio beam station at Maple Creek? Is it the intention to move that station from that town north?
Yes, that is the intention; the field will be moved north.
Both the station and the field?
Yes.
What type of ship is it planned to fly on the trans-Canada route, and what designating insignia does the minister plan to place upon them?
Standard equipment will be the Lockheed 14; the designation will be TCA with a maple leaf.
How many passengers do they carry? Are they over-night planes?

The planes have fourteen seats; that would be twelve passengers. There is no sleeping accommodation; but they are very comfortable planes, widely used in the western section of the United States for overnight work.

Is it the plan of the Trans-Canada Air Lines to fly bigger ships later, depending on how much traffic there is; and, if so, will they be sleeper planes? The minister I believe, mentioned it is an over-night flight from Winnipeg to Montreal.

The size of the planes of
course will depend entirely on the density of traffic. I hope the traffic will soon warrant larger planes, and, if so, we shall certainly provide sleeping accommodation.

I notice the amount to
be spent under this item this year is approximately the same as last; therefore one can assume that there will be steady development of the airways. I think I mentioned last year when the estimates were before the committee that we are not naturally an air-minded people in Canada yet, as far as passengers are concerned. That is strange in view of the fact that we are the nation which has flown more freight than any other twro nations together in the world, and as I have already mentioned, has been most successful as far as pilots are concerned. The success of this system will depend entirely on the amount of traffic carried. Bearing in mind that we. as a people, are not particularly air-minded, has the minister anything to tell the committee in regard to projected advertising to bring to the attention of the people of this dominion the fact that they will have available an air transport system which is efficient, rapid and safe?

What has been done in
regard to the tying-in of the present northern Ontario routes for flying freight? As the minister well knows, and as I have just stated, we are flying more freight in northern Ontario and the northern parts of the prairie provinces as well, than any other two nations in the world. Is there any tie-in of the Trans-Canada lines planned with these present private lines? Is it the intention that they remain as private lines, functioning as they have in the past?

The private lines of course
are functioning now, and the Trans-Canada is not. But the Trans-Canada will have stops at the main air bases from which these private lines fly, and there will be traffic arrangements with them. We are not interfering in any way with the private flying that is now being done, and will not do so except to cooperate in exchange of traffic. But our line is very favourably based to tie in with these operations.

Last year the minister
stated that it was the intention of Trans-Canada Air Lines to have no service between Toronto and Montreal, the two largest population centres in the dominion. It seemed strange to some at that time that that was to be the case. To-night the minister mentioned that the route from Montreal would pass through Toronto. Does he mean that Trans-Canada planes will fly to Ottawa, to Reay, to Toronto and to Winnipeg, or is it the intention to fly direct from Montreal to Winnipeg and run a feeder line to and from Toronto as was suggested last year? And is it suggested that there will be a direct line from Toronto to Montreal without going roundabout?

I covered that earlier; planes will leave Montreal for Ottawa, Killaloe, Reay, Toronto, and then from Toronto back to Reay and on to North Bay and the west. As the traffic develops, we hope there will be sufficient for a plane from Montreal to Vancouver and another from Toronto to Vancouver, in which event there will undoubtedly be a short service between Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal. But the air fields that I have
mentioned will be those used for that service, being expensive fields and fully equipped. No purpose would be served by trying a shorter route; with the high speed equipment we are using the saving of distance would be fully offset by the slower type of plane that would have to be used on the shorter route.

Has the minister any idea
of the flying schedule that will be planned between, say Toronto, Montreal and Winnipeg, or Toronto and Winnipeg?

Yes. The present plan which I think would suit the Post Office Department is to leave Montreal at eight o'clock, be in Ottawa about eighty-thirty, Toronto about nine-thirty, leave for the west about ten o'clock, arriving at Vancouver the next day at noon.
What is the situation with respect to the transatlantic service. What are the plans for that service?

Test flights were carried out last summer with equipment which happened to be available, and those flights proved to be very successful. From the data collected, the planes which will actually be used in the routes are now being developed, and it is expected that further flights will take place as soon as spring arrives. I think it is quite within the range of possibility that mail will be carried on that route before the end of this season, although I cannot say that definitely. We have had information from England and the United States indicating that there is a possibility of that being carried out. I may say that everything which has been found out to date with respect to that route is entirely favourable, and we think it is only a matter of a year or two before the service will be in steady operation.
What service is to be given, and what length of time will be required to fly the route?
Something less than twenty-four hours from Montreal to Southampton. I believe the service will be twice a week, each way.
What plans are being made for a route from British Columbia to Australia, New Zealand and the orient? Has that been under consideration?
No.

What amount has been expended to date on the airport at Killaloe? Is the work completed, and, if not, what is the contemplated expenditure this year?
