was $8,488; the expenditure to date in the development of land was $86,364, and the estimated expenditure to complete, which will be carried out this year is $11,720.

As the minister is aware, the auxiliary municipal airport for Toronto is situated at Malton, in the county I represent. We are very proud of the airport, and have been told on many occasions that it is perhaps one of the greatest airports on the continent. I have heard with much interest and satisfaction statements which have been made by some hon. members concerning other airports in Canada. I should like the minister to assure me that the Malton airport ranks with high favour among the various ports of Canada. Perhaps he would be good enough to say whether or not the Malton airport is at present highest in standing of all those in the dominion.
The city of Toronto pays for it.
There is no airport at Malton yet; but it is well spoken of, and I think when it is completed it will be a very fine airport.

I am sure other hon. members from Nova Scotia were disappointed this evening when we heard that the trans-Canada air line would end at Moncton, instead of Halifax. I have before me a map published a short time ago by one of the departments, in which the Trans-Canada Air Lines are shown as going to Halifax. I am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce will be disappointed to get word to-night that that is not so, because in the publication "Canada, 1938" the map appears, and in a statement signed by the minister I find:
The hand book is designed to serve two purposes. To those outside of Canada it will give a well rounded picture of the Canadian situation from Atlantic to Pacific. In Canada itself it will help to provide a better basis of information for dealing with current problems.
My first question is this: Is it now proposed to change the name of the Trans-Canada Air Lines to conform to the actual situation of the proposed route? My second question is, coming down to serious matters: What has been the experience as to fog conditions at Stanley, in Hants county, where intermediate landing fields are being developed?
All I can say is that it is a trifle better than Halifax, but not as good as Moncton.

I do not wish to say much concerning the eastern terminus of the Trans-Canada Air Lines. I believe, however, that
TMr. McCann.]
the minister and his department might well be commended at least by some hon. members from New Brunswick for selecting Moncton as the terminus. It is well known that Moncton and its vicinity are free from fog, and it is known, too, that when a few years ago the Italian airmen were selecting a port to land their ships on the Atlantic coast, they selected Shediac, because it was more free from fog than any other part of the Atlantic coast in the vicinity.
Just then.
I do not think the minister is to be condemned for having selected Moncton as an airport. I am inclined to think he should be commended.

The hon. member who has just taken his seat has made a statement which I believe is absolutely correct. It appears to me that there is a lack of candidness, not on the part of the minister, but on the part of those who are supplying him with information. The crux of the situation is that, so far as the east is concerned, the trans-Canada airways will go from Shediac, in crossing the Atlantic. No transatlantic liners make Shediac a terminus. The Minister of Transport is responsible for the Canadian National Railways, the largest single transcontinental system in Canada or the United States. When the St. Lawrence is closed by ice, Halifax is the natural port; I do not say that in a spirit of rancour or to cause discord.
I will say that all Canadian Pacific ships going to Saint John, carrying passengers, land first at Halifax to drop passengers and mail. Are the passengers on Atlantic liners landing at Halifax to be told that they will be taken care of by some fantastic private company, and probably sent off into eternity before they reach their destination at Moncton or Montreal? I believe we are entitled to this information from the minister, or the officers of his department. Those officers are highly paid; therefore they must be highly efficient, and he must have all the information necessary to give each hon. member a full knowledge of what he is going to do with the trans-Canada airway system.
The Minister of Transport stated that the airways were to be taken care of by the Canadian National Railways, and that Mr. Hungerford, the head of the railways, is to be head of the airways. At first we were going to have fifty-one per cent of the stock; and the balance was going to be given to the public. However, so far not one dollar's worth has been sold to the public. It all remains with the Canadian National Railways. These gentlemen-President Hungerford, his

Supply-Transport-Airways
officers and board of directors-have padlocked the whole Canadian National railway system, and it would take all the tons of dynamite used in the late war to get satisfactory information from that president and board of directors. They simply tell us it is none of our business. They are a corporation within themselves-and a corporation is not supposed to have any soul. But we have souls. We are responsible to the people who have sent us here. We are entitled to the information, and we should get it. We are not living in Russia. We are not living in Italy. We are not living in Germany. We are here, in a young and great democratic country, with infinite possibilities ahead of us. The democracy of this country is demonstrated by the fact that there are so many different groups outside the " two great parties " that have always been the leaders of the people.
A short time ago the Minister of Transport made a damaging statement with reference to air travel from Moncton to Halifax. He stated that there was too much fog and that too many people had been killed. When I asked him for detailed information, his answer was a smile. That information has not yet been given. I do not expect this information to-night, but I think the minister should assure me and other members of the committee that he will have the officers of his department tabulate all accidents which have happened since he has been head of the department. This tabulation should show the number of accidents that happened in the air, the number that happened when planes were approaching the landing ports, and the number that happened after the planes had landed. With that information before us we shall then know whether the statement should be retracted. I am quite sure that when the minister has that information he will be only too willing to retract his statement. It is a black eye, and we get too many of them down in the maritimes and particularly at the port of Halifax.
I do not want to say anything further about the port of Saint John, other than to say to my hon. friend that there is ten times as much fog in Saint John as ever comes into Halifax. The fog is off Halifax harbour; it does not come into the harbour. Flying would be perfectly safe if you had a radio beam. I can remember the first trip the minister took. He started off in thunder and lightning and had to come back when the beam was not working. They got it working and he took another try, landed in Winnipeg and finally arrived safely in Vancouver.
I should like him to reverse that trip. I want him to start, not in thunder and lightning, but on a starry night. I want him to fly east and I know he will find that the conditions he spoke of to-night do not exist. This trans-Canada system should extend from Vancouver to Halifax. That was my understanding of the undertaking when it was first mooted. It may be all right for the flyers if they are going to stop at Moncton or go down to Shediac. The Italian flyers flew there and they considered it the best place possible. They did not know anything about Canada and they had better get Mussolini to let them come back again. I am reminded of the famous flyer who landed at Toronto and then said he would never come back again. That was a damaging statement to be made by a pilot of outstanding ability.
I do not want to prolong this discussion, but I want to remind the minister that Nova Scotia is not being considered as part of this trans-Canada airway scheme. We do not want to be sectional, but we feel we are entitled to the same consideration as has been given to. other parts of Canada. My hon. friend said to me in conversation that this year Halifax has had the greatest tonnage in shipping in her history. That may be so, but that does not mean that employment is given to our men. Many of the liners anchor back of " George island," and the tenders go out to meet them; the only money paid out is to the pilots and by way of port dues. The stevedores and dockworkers still remain at home and many of them, as well as their families, I sadly fear, are hungry to-night in their homes.
These conditions must be ameliorated. I think I speak for other hon. members from Nova Scotia as they spoke for themselves tonight, when I say that we are not going to put up with this treatment. We are not speaking in any narrow sense, but we feel that we should start right on this matter. AVe started wrong on the railways, so let us keep the airways out of the Canadian National Railways. The only information we can get about the railways as to money expended is the capital expenditures. If the bookkeeping for this system is to be the same as that used in the Canadian National Railways under President Hungerford and his board of directors, then there will be a fog all over Canada. We shall know less about the airways than we do about the railways, and about the railways we know practically nothing, apart from capital expenditures to better the system.
I do not make these remarks in a personal way; but in view of what has happened in the past, considering the present and looking down the vista of the future, I think we should start this thing right. I believe this has

Supply-Transport-Airways

been exemplified by the action taken by the governments of the various provinces in connection with the amendments to the British North America Act and the righting of the wrongs that have been done under that act. Now is the time to deal with this matter and get it on a solid foundation. Then, with the expert knowledge which the minister has at his disposal, we shall be able to deal intelligently with the voting of these vast sums of money. The government seems to be disinterested as far as Nova Scotia is concerned, but I think we are entitled to get the information when, where and how-I mean "h-o-w", not the hon. minister, "H-o-w-e".

We have had a long discussion on a subject with which few of us are familiar. I congratulate the hon. member who has just sat down upon the pertinent remarks he has made. Attention should be given to what he has said. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North who said that he thought it would be a good thing to leave this matter to the minister. If I were in the place of the minister I believe I would select the best possible advice and operate these flying boats or flying ships from the places where the most business could be obtained. I would want to lose as little money as possible and make air travel as safe as I could, and I would pay very little attention to hon. members who wanted to give advice, such as has been given to-night. We know that every hon. member would like to have a flying ship landed in his own back yard.

I have no back yard. I live in the eastern gateway of Canada. We all know what is carved in the stone on the front
of this house of parliament:
The wholesome sea is at her gates,
Her gates both east and west.
Change the government and all the services will be paying.

I would not promise that; I am not giving to making promises, and if I were the minister I would be making very few. He has been asked many questions tonight to which no man can give an intelligent answer. I am not blaming him, because people are asking him questions that no man can answer. The minister is telling the committee what he thinks might happen, but it is purely conjecture, to be taken for what it is worth.

Would it not be
possible for the trans-Canada air route to be wholly across Canada, without going over any part of the United States? My second question is:	What proportion of the cost of airports is borne by the municipalities and what by the dominion government?
Has the company established a schedule of passenger rates yet, and, if so, what approximately will be the rate from Montreal to Vancouver?
Airplane travel costs, roughly, six cents a mile. The matter of rates has not been brought to my attention, but I dare say some people are studying it. I could not answer the question.

I would like to take the
minister and the committee back to the coast again, as we have now spent considerable time in the east. I think it was the policy of the department, when the idea of the trans-Canada service was first considered, to establish emergency landing fields about thirty miles apart. In the fall of 1934 officers of the department made a survey by plane, and selected landing fields particularly in the southern part of British Columbia. The minister mentioned two of them to-night. One of them was the emergency landing field at Hope, and the other was the emergency landing field at Langley. In that survey there was an emergency landing field at Hope, another one thirty miles west at Chilliwack, and thirty miles further west took them to Langley airport. A number of people, including those who own private airplanes and do considerable flying, are of the opinion that the department has made a mistake in abandoning Chilliwack landing field and taking
up Langley. I am sure if the minister personally visited the two places-I know he went over that district one day, but he was too high up in the clouds to see the location of the two fields-he would realize the superiority of Chilliwack. First, let me point out that the Chilliwack landing field is used today, and has been for some time, by eight planes. It consists of 160 acres; does not require drainage, but it might require a little finishing and the putting in of runways. In 1935 the government secured an option on it for $16,000, or $100 an acre, and that item appeared in the estimates for two sessions; but immediately on civil aviation being transferred to the new department over which the minister presides, that item was eliminated from the estimates.
I find now that work is being proceeded with at the Langley airport, where ninety acres of land have been purchased at a cost of $24,411.60; I do not know how they get those odd figures. This figures out at $272 an acre, and they have expended on the field to date $48,437. In other words, the port so far has cost $72,848, and the estimated amount required to complete the field is $15,925, making a total cost of $88,773. That is the picture we have of the Langley field, and it would not be too bad if it was a field that airplanes could land on; but airmen who are passing up and down tell me that it certainly would be some great emergency before they would ever undertake to land there. The field is located at the foot of a hill, and is right in the fog belt, as bad if not a worse fog belt than Vancouver, and the field subject to flood. I hav e an extract from an independent paper published in the district, which I think I had better read to show the committee what the people there think of this field:
If the latter amount-
That is the $72,848 already spent:
has been spent to get the field into its present condition, most observers will doubt the statement that $16,000 will complete it. The condition of the field was well expressed the other day by a strong Liberal when he said that there was too much water on it for land planes and not enough for sea planes. From the field's appearance during recent weeks it would require a rotary drill to find any plane that might be forced to land anywhere in the 90-acre block Then there is the matter of fog which so frequently envelopes the field. Experts in these matters may know what they are about but to the layman the demonstration so far lacks much of what might be expressed in terms of practicability.
As regards fog conditions, I repeat that I believe, if the minister himself had seen those two fields and inquired personally about them, he would not have hesitated one minute to
Supply-Transport-Airways

choose the Chilliwack field. Why has the Langley field been, chosen? First, political pressure on the minister.
Bought in 1934, was it not?
That does not make any difference. Options were taken on all these fields in 1935.
1934, I think.

The reply to the question is 1935. The first was 1935. An option was taken at Chilliwack at the same time on one hundred and sixty acres. I am not blaming the minister personally. I would not accuse him of doing this. I believe there was considerable pressure brought to bear on him from the minister for British Columbia and from the hon. member for New Westminster, and I believe he has been misinformed by the officers of his department. I have asked for correspondence, which has not been brought down here yet, although the order for return passed the house on the fourteenth instant.
Before I left Chilliwack for the east, a letter was read to the executive of the board of trade, which reached there through Liberal channels, stating that the reason the development there was not proceeded with was that conditions in the Chilliwack district are the same as in Vancouver and Langley. That is absolutely false. Eight machines have been taking off and flying from that field during last year. One has kept a careful log which shows that there was not one day during 1937 when they could not land and take off from that field. What do we know about the Vancouver field? And Langley? Any one who travels by automobile knows that he can leave Vancouver in sunshine, get in the fog belt at Langley and break out again within ten or fifteen miles of Chilliwack field. I am advised the United air lines could not land in Vancouver from December 3 to December 23; that was but one period among others when they could not land. I say to the minister that the log which was kept last year shows that this Chilliwack field is not in the fog belt, and there is not an air man who travels that country, not a man who drives a car up and down to Vancouver, but will tell him that the fog reaches to within ten or fifteen miles west of the ChilliwTack airport. That fog is like a wall. These men have taken off in their machines, gone over that wall, over that ceiling and back again. I wish the minister would look personally into this.
The department is going to spend $90,000 on a field in the Langley district. The expenditure of the money will do considerable good as far as employment is concerned, but

it is the opinion of a number of air men in both Chilliwack and district that they will never be able to use that field, whereas the other one is being used to-day. That option can be renewed at $16,000, and if it were necessary to spend another $10,000 the cost would not be within a third of what the Langley field is costing. I say without hesitation that there has been political pressure to have this field established at Langley. Some Liberals in my riding have not hesitated to say, " The reason you have not got the field is because you elected a Conservative member." I do not blame the minister personally; I do not believe he would consider the political angle in connection with a policy of establishing an air line across Canada. I do not think he would say, " Here is a Conservative constituency; we cannot put our line through that, we will dodge down through the United States and back again to miss it." I believe that if the matter had been left to the minister personally; if he had gone in and looked over the situation, there would have been no doubt about his decision. I believe the department will have to come to the Chilliwack field. It was mentioned at a meeting in Vancouver the other day, that if they arrived at Vancouver in a fog, they would likely have to return to Lethbridge. I believe they fly at a height of 16,000 feet. I have done a little travelling by air, and I understand that what they do, in case of fog, is to land as closely as they can to the terminus and from there take other transportation. We -were in hopes that the Chilliwack field would serve for that purpose, a field of 160 acres which has been used for a number of years.

No.

If we have made a mistake in choosing a field out there we shall very soon realize it. Once the planes are operating daily, if we need additional facilities the fact will become quite obvious and we shall have to look about for them. But I think at the moment we are so close to having an actual demonstration of the situation there, through every day flying, that we should wait and get that information.
I am sure the local air men would be pleased to permit the minister to land on that field some day when he finds he cannot reach Vancouver.
Thank you very much.
Because they tell me the largest plane that reaches the coast could land on that field to-day.

I am sure the minister must regard the statement which has just been made as one of great seriousness. Are we to throw away eighty or ninety thousand dollars of this country's money? It is not a question of finding out a mistake and remedying it; the question is, Shall we throw away the money now that the facts have been stated? I have been at the coast several times this last year, and undoubtedly the view prevails that that place is entirely too wet to make a decent airport, at least for a land plane, and there is not enough water for a sea plane. The hon. member has brought that to the attention of the minister and has said to him: This merits investigation before further public money is expended. A man who certainly never mixes in politics, talking about business and business administration and the capacity of the minister as a business man, said he was surprised that the minister would permit this thing to be done. I wonder if the minister realizes just what is meant by it? It means we are going to throw away eighty or ninety thousand dollars on a place which cannot be made into an airport, and it cannot be made into an airport for two good reasons: One is fog, and the other is damp; one is water, the other is the condition of the air. I submit to the minister that if ever there was a case brought to the attention of the head of the department that merited the closest investigation before a single additional dollar is spent, this is that case. The minister knows perfectly well that when we had to acquire these sites away back in 1934 and 1935, some in the early part of 1935, and some in connection with relief works, what was done was not to content ourselves with taking one option; options were taken on more than one site, and then investigations were made in several cases for the purpose of ascertaining which was the better or the best, as the case might be.
I put this to the minister as a business man. In the conduct of his business, if it were represented to him by reputable people that conditions were such that it would be impossible to utilize a particular property for the purpose for which it was acquired, would he proceed without making further investigation? From what I know of him as a business executive he would not do so. To-day he is a minister, and all the pressure in the world, from all the friends in the world, should not permit him to go forward with an expenditure of public moneys without satisfying himself that that is the better site. Any other action on his part would, under our system of government, certainly place him in a most difficult position. It would not, of course, if a very large number of supporters stated that
his conclusions were sound, whatever they might be. That is the essence of party government, but it is not the essence of government if the minister is to utilize the vast experience and wide knowledge he has as a business man in determining what is the best thing that can be done for the state in the expenditure of public moneys.
One word more to my friends from the maritime provinces. However difficult it may be, I never forget that I was born there; and when I realize that all the members from the lower provinces, except one, support the government in power, I realize how difficult their position is with respect to this matter. But I put this to the minister and ask him to balance it up on this basis: If you are warranted in providing a subsidy for the operation of an air service between Edmonton and the Yukon, having a population to be served with mail as limited as it is, do you think for a single moment that the maritimes should be treated in this manner? Apply that test, just that simple, single test. Later I am going to direct attention to something that came to my own notice, which would not be tolerated in western Canada. Do you realize that passengers, in order to board a train going to Saint John from Moncton-and this applies to aged people as well as the young-[DOT] have to climb over a platform on a standing train? How long would that be tolerated in western Canada? And yet that is the condition which exists in the maritimes. That is the reason the maritimes complain, and properly so, about the treatment they receive.
I wrote to both the general manager and the president with respect to this treatment. The answer was, "Oh well, it has been going on a long time." Of course it has, and the people there have suffered and have endured it. But we would not tolerate it. Take the old station at Toronto. Everyone knows that the minute the train came in, it was cut in two in order that passengers might cross on level tracks. I saw an old lady down in the maritimes lifting herself up slowly, without assistance, over a platform on a standing ear of the maritime express and then going down the other side in order to get on the train that would take her to Saint John. I asked, "Don't you split these trains?" I was told that they never do.
Surely it is no political consideration that urges me to make these observations, for we have no supporters from that part of the country. I would point out, however, that that sort of thing should not be tolerated. Here we find the oldest part of confederation treated in this manner, and we are told that

there is plenty of money provided for a new line, a private enterprise, from Edmonton to the Yukon, a mail subsidy being given, when we know what the population in that part of the country is. We know what the population is in the Yukon and between the Yukon and Edmonton, and we know also that there are hundreds of thousands of people in the maritime provinces. We know that the largest steel industry in Canada is situated in Nova Scotia; and the people of that province, the people of Saint John and all the community that lies around it will be told, "Oh well, some day somebody will come along and give you a service and we will help them along with some assistance." That is not fair; it is not equitable, having regard to what I have said about the expenditure of public moneys and in view of statements made in this chamber by a member of this house. If it rested on that alone it might be said to be political, but consult any business man you please. That is the situation. Let us try to see if we cannot lift this thing up a little at least out of the fog of politics into the purer air of business transactions.

As regards the Langley Prairie airport, I inherited that. When it came to my attention, the land had been bought and the contract let to develop it. We let no new contract there and I know nothing about it personally. My officers tell me that it is the best piece of land in that vicinity. Since definite statements are made that it is not a suitable place, on the next occasion on which I go to Vancouver I shall personally examine it, and no new contract will be placed there in the meantime.
Let us understand the maritime situation. I am giving the maritime provinces the best system I know how to give them. I am not giving them a second-rate system. What is the alternative? Suppose we ran a high speed plane from Montreal to Halifax. You could hardly pass by Saint John if you went to Halifax. Well, suppose we stopped at Saint John. It is estimated by my department that such a route would have an operating efficiency of sixty per cent; we would complete about sixty per cent of the scheduled trips. With the route we have we can complete at least ninety per cent. Ninety days out of every hundred we have delivered our mail in Moncton. We have it in Moncton, anyway. If it is impossible to fly to Halifax any particular day, we can put it on the train and get it in within a few hours.
But there is no assurance of a movement to Halifax or to Saint John either. That is the whole trouble.
What nonsense that is.
Thank you.

Coming to the city of Regina, what do we do? We call for a specification for a route to serve the five prairie cities. We specify the type of equipment and the speed of the planes. We specify the number of stops to be made, and we require a guarantee of at least ninety-two per cent efficiency. We have said to the aviators of the world, "This is the equipment we must have; this is the schedule; this is the efficiency required. Bid us a price on mail at which you will perform that service."
Has that been done at Halifax?
Not yet.
That is the point.

When we are prepared for a service from Moncton we shall then similarly call for tenders from Moncton to Charlottetown, from Moncton to Sydney, from Moncton to Halifax and from Moncton to Saint John; and we shall specify the equipment. It will not be cheap equipment any more than it is in Saskatchewan; it will be just as good equipment, as comfortable from the passenger standpoint. However, the distances are short and the equipment will not be speedy, because such equipment is not required there. It will be equipment of the type that will land on the sort of field which can be built in Halifax and Saint John, the type of equipment that can be manoeuvred in difficult weather conditions; and we shall have a beam into each of these cities, so that flying will be done on just as good a beam as there is in the mainland operation. We shall have suitable facilities to handle passengers and mail at these points. We find, however, that with a small operation it is better to have private enterprise than public.
It should be all one enterprise from Vancouver to Halifax.

If the maritimes feel that we should have government operation there, we shall have government operation. Personally I think they would be better served the other way. However, I do not suppose the expense to the dominion government would be very much different, and I would be prepared to discuss with the maritime delegation having Trans-Canada Air Lines operate those auxiliary services from the centre at Moncton. But it is perfect nonsense for any member to say here that we are not giving the maritime provinces the best. The reason we are stopping at

Supply-Transport-Airways
Moncton is that it is the best thing for the maritime provinces. If it were better to stop at Halifax we would stop at Halifax; if Saint John were better we would stop at Saint John. But what nonsense it is to say that we are not giving the maritime provinces the best it is possible to give, consistent with the service we are giving any other part of Canada. I want to make it clear that nothing of the kind is intended and nothing of the kind will be done.
A United States line offered to run and did run from Boston to Halifax.
Why doesn't it still?
Because in the days of the old government we did not want to make ourselves dependent on a United States company.

Quite right, and we are not going to either. However, we have a line pushing up as far as Bangor and anxious to go further. There will be ways to get to Boston from Halifax, because they fly from Boston to Montreal in two hours.
It was suggested they could fly from Montreal to Saint John and across the bay of Fundy straight to Halifax.
That could be done, but it is fog operation; it would not be good.
Well, there is difference of opinion as to that.

However, we are going to see that the maritime provinces are properly served just as soon as it is possible to provide that service. But we are taking the things as we found them; when we took the department over we found the fields further advanced in the west and capable of being completed in a shorter time. We believed that the way to get the line in operation was to start operation, and we found that the quickest way to start operating was to concentrate on the completion of the fields from Winnipeg west. Now we are at the point that we can start operating that section. We are going to work east just as rapidly as we can. By midsummer we shall be in Montreal. It is possible we shall be at Moncton and on to Halifax at the end of this season; but I doubt it; I think it is more likely to be the beginning of next season.

I am obliged to the minister for talking about nonsense. I am not directing his attention to the fact that it is not a parliamentary expression; I am content that he should make the statement. But I
think he should realize this, that they were running an air line from Moncton to Charlottetown four years ago-
And they are running it to-day.

Exactly. And the west
that he talks about-and I live there-had not developed these lines. What is more, they have been running to Halifax during the last four years. And what is more, they have been running from Montreal to Moncton during the last four years.
An occasional trip.

Yes; I am only indicating that the feasibility of it is established; that is the point. There is no question about its not being easy to do, or anything of that sort. And we have reached the point that we have made no arrangement whatever that contemplates air mail service being made available in the provinces of Nova Scotia or New Brunswick except as the mail arrives at Moncton for distribution.
Quite right.

That is the story, and I say that is not in keeping with the other plans which have been placed before this country. While I owe only the allegiance that a man has by reason of birth in a particular locality, I do not think it is quite fair that we should spend all our effort in endeavouring to establish what they call feeder lines and other lines. Calgary is to be in the position of being on a feeder line. Large sums of money have been expended there, power and lighthouses established, routes surveyed, and now they say, "Well, the old field is not satisfactory for modem planes." And they need something else. The Department of National Defence, on which we have spent a large sum to provide an air field, is not going to cooperate with the Department of Transport for the purpose of using that piece of ground, bought by the crown, for the purpose of an air field. It is not going to be used because the Department of National Defence say it is not consonant with their dignity. I say that is wrong. I think the minister realizes that there is something wrong about that, when he says, " I asked the Minister of National Defence to do so and so but he does not want to let me have it." Have we reached that stage in this country when in regard to a field bought and equipped with the taxpayers' money, used for national defence, and with room enough to enable it to be used for civil aviation as well, they say, " Oh no, we cannot do that." Cooperation certainly means something better than that

The minister knows this committee, this house would support him if he took the position that he must have the use of that field.
Why have two fields in one community? Why have one airport in Calgary for civil aviation and another for military aviation? It is there on top of the hill; atmospheric conditions are excellent; all that is necessary to do is to start a machine down the runway and get it off or to land there. I admit that there are certain strategic considerations which have to do with military airports, but they do not arise in connection with this matter. I say the minister would be warranted in taking a much stronger stand than to say, " The Minister of National Defence does not want me to go there." Well, the people want it; they paid for it and they have a right to it. Is it thus to remain idle-that is what it would mean practically-not be utilized for commercial purposes and the carrying of mail? After all we have done in connection with the expenditures for airports and lighting, I think that is wrong.
I am sure if the minister were similarly situated with respect to Port Arthur he would expect that some such arrangement would be made to permit this splendid airport to be used by both branches of our air service, civil aviation on the one hand and military on the other. I am sure the minister would not regard that as nonsense in business, from what I know of his capacity as a business man. In his business before he came into this house or since, he would not; or in the development of any work he has had to do, whether it were the preparation of a site for an elevator or the construction of an elevator, he would expect to coordinate every bit of facilities to attain the end he has in mind. All we want to do is to coordinate the airport facilities for the double purpose of civil aviation on the one hand and military on the other.

Would the minister let us know how far the officers of his department will go in cooperating with civic authorities who are trying to choose a site for an airport? Will they advise and help and give the benefit of their experience and skill?
Yes, we shall be very glad to cooperate with any city that cares to have our cooperation. Whether we can assist them financially depends on how it works in with the general scheme.
Is it under this item that the employment of the gentlemen whom the minister mentioned the other evening at the Chateau Laurier would come?
No.

I think this item had better remain over until the next day. There are some things to be said.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
